Now, we find that $16,900,000 worth of Klondike gold, every dollar of it Canadian

gold, and that $667,000 of British Columbia gold, went to the Seattle assay office, every dollar's worth of which, should, if there had been an assay office at Victoria or Vancouver, have gone into our own hands. The miners would have sold it to the mint or assay office and would have spent enormous sums of money buying their supplies in these cities. The paper also goes on to speak of what they are expecting this year :
It is also interesting to note the confirmation of the Post-Intelligencer's figure on the output of the Klondike for 1900. This was given at $20,000,000. The popular estimate ranged to $25,000,000 and higher. But the officers of the Yukon police, having charge of the collection of royalties on the output

I want the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) to listen to this, or is it the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton).
-reported only $11,752,560, while the records of the Dawson custom-house brought the total only to about $14,000,000. The fact now appears that the Seattle assay office received from Klondike $16,946,437.08, and sufficient bullion is known to be now laying in safe deposit in this city to advance the total to more than $20,000,000.
We, therefore, find that the officers of the government in the Yukon, in collecting the royalty, have been fooled by the miners to the extent of nearly $9,000,000, which has gone into American territory, and has paid no tax to the Dominion treasury. Here is another :
Stream of Gold from the North.
This is dated April 7th of this year. It says :
More than $22,000,000 worth of gold-dust and bullion, out of the total output of thirty-three and a half millions mined in Alaska, the Klondike, British Columbia and the north-western states, passed through the Seattle assay office during the year 1900.
It goes on to say :
These are sums the colossal proportions of which, cannot readily be grasped or understood by the average man, but which, if handled on Wall street or some other eastern financial centre, would be treated and heralded the world over as phenomenal. Here, however, in the land of gold and plenty, millions are handled and talked, of with the nonchalance of speculators in breadstuffs or provisions, and form part of the everyday business transactions.
The present season is already far enough advanced to enable a fair estimate to be made of the probable output for 1901, and although many reports are coming out of Alaska and the Klondike, which place the increase in the output at fully 50 per cent greater than last year among the more conservative mine operators of the various districts, the belief is gaining ground that the increase over last year's output, from all sources, will be about one-third ; that is to say, where the 1900 output footed up a total of $33,590,000, this year it is expected to reach a total of $44,700,000.
So that we find that according to past operations the output is going to be $44,-129J
000,000 of gold taken out of that far western country and out of the Klondike, and it is estimated that from the Klondike $27,000,000 will be taken this year. I would ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) not to delay any longer in bringing this matter to an issue. The inference to be drawn from the hon. gentleman's speech in Montreal, I presume, is that the mint will be built in Montreal. If that is the case I must protest against such a proposal. The proper place to build the mint is in the province of British Columbia.
Hear, hear.
An hon. gentleman says ' hear, hear ' in a sarcastic manner.
No, no.

Oh, I see where it comes from. I am glad to think that somebody is endorsing my statements. I will now show the reason why the gold goes to Seattle. The following is taken from the report published of the interviews and correspondence between the provincial and Dominion governments :
The reason why the gold is taken to Seattle is because the United States assay office there buys it at a higher price than is or can be paid for it in British Columbia. The gold is bought in Seattle at exactly the same rate as if handed in to the mint at Washington, the United States government paying the express and insurance charges on the bars from the branch office to the mint, so that the only deduction made from the gross value of the dust is the assay charge.
Gold brought to Victoria or Vancouver is taken to a bank and by the bank sent to the British Columbia government assay office. The charges are practically the same as the Seattle assay office, but the bank in British Columbia has to send the bars to the mint, and in addition to again paying assay charges has to defray the cost of expressage, insurance and other charges, and at the same time provide for a fair business profit. The price obtained for gold dust taken to Seattle is higher, therefore, than that paid in British Columbia cities by the above charges, which amount to about 2 per cent on the gross value of the gold.
To meet this competition British Columbia must be in a position to offer at least as good terms as Seattle, and the provincial mineralogist makes the following suggestion, as an alternative proposal, in case the mint should not be established in British Columbia.
Of course, we know it is going to be, but still, I read it.
The government of British Columbia to be authorized to purchase, as agents for the Dominion government, all gold offered, at the same rate as that paid by the United States government; the local government establishing the necessary offices and being responsible for all losses. The gold to be handed to an agent appointed by the Dominion government, and the weight and fineness of the gold to be guaranteed by the British Columbia government.
The provincial mineralogist points out that, of course, the assay fees will not begin to pay

the expenses of an assay office, and the difference would have to be borne by the local government, who would alst>
be responsible for the gold and the correctness of the weight and assays.
The Dominion government would have to pay the expressage, interest and other charges on value during transit.
It will cost the government very little, I think, to turn that magnificent flow of yellow metal from Seattle to our own cities of Victoria and Vancouver. There is no doubt about it that if we have a mint or an assay office inj British Columbia, the miners will come down to get coin for their gold. Let 'me say that in my opinion the proper place for that mint is the city of Victoria. That city is the capital of the province, it is the headquarters of the Pacific naval station, and it is the port from which the largest part of the shipping starts for the northern country whence the gold comes. We all know the immense strides which Seattle has made during the last few years, and I can safely say that progress is due to nothing more nor less than the stream of gold which has been pouring into it from the north. The government have promised to act. Let them act at once so that not another moment will be lost in the effort towards securing for us that our own gold shall be brought to our own country.
Just one word in regard to; the necessity that exists for the government inquiring into the possibilities of Canada doing a large trade with Siberia. My colleague and I have already spoken to the Min-Inster of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) in regard to this matter, and he has promised to look into it. I trust that he will send some trustworthy and intelligent man to inquire into our trade possibilities with Siberia, as he has done in the case of the Latin American Republics. I think the minister will find that Canada has a good chance of inaugurating a profitable trade with the newly developed country of Siberia. The Americans of San Francisco and of Portland, Ore., have already entered upon that commercial field. They have sent several ship loads of goods there and they believe that they will be able to do a large trade with Siberia. If the people of San Francisco can succeed in that why cannot Canadians ou the Pacific coast succeed as well. I throw this out as a hint to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he should not allow the grass to grow under his feet but that he should get a good and reliable man to look into this question.
I have spoken already this session upon the lumber duties, the) Indian reserves, the Lepers and other matters which interest the people of British Columbia, so that I need not refer to them on this occasion. The people of that province have not agitated for their rights in any undue way ; they have always addressed themselves in a pro-

per manner to the government for these things which they think they should have, but patience is a virtue which may get worn out in time. They are a long-suffering people in British Columbia ; they are not professional agitators ; they have been patient under their grievances, but I must say that I think we have about got to the end of our tether in the exercise of patience. If this government will do justice to British Columbia in the manner I have indicated the government will find that they will be creating in that Pacific province a vast market for the products of eastern Canada, and they will not have a more loyal and hard-working population in all Canada, than they will have in British Columbia.
Hear, hear.

I have but a few words to say in answer to the speech of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior). Although the hon. gentleman stated in his exordium that British Columbia was suffering under great grievances, and although in his peroration he repeated the same statement, I think the House will be of opinion after listening to the general tenor of the hon. gentleman's remarks, that the grievances referred to are not so very serious after all. With regard to the mint, for instance, and the assay office, the hon. gentleman discovered he had no grievance whatever. As has just been intimated by the hon. Finance Minister the government propose to implement the promises which have been made upon this subject and resolutions will be introduced to that effect at a very early date. As to the ship subsidies, that is a new policy that requires some consideration before the government entertains it The chief argument of my hon. friend was that a Bill is before Congress offering such a subsidy to American shipping, but Congress has hesitated a long time before! coming to any conclusion, aud, therefore, I think, we can very well allow the matter to remain where it is for the present. The fishery question has! two sides to it. The remedy proposed by the hon. gentleman for the grievances of the canners-and I must say these grievances are of long standing-is to transfer the control of the fisheries in the Columbia river to the province of British Columbia. My hon. friend will find on reflection that such a remedy could not be thought of for a moment, because under the British North America Act the government and parliament is powerless in the matter. We cannot divest the province of any control which it has under that Act, nor can we divest the Dominion of its control over any matter assigned to it by our constitution. If my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries were here, he would have some observations to show that there are two sides to this question.

The main complaint which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior) makes is one which is very much to the credit of his own province. It is that the people of British Columbia contribute largely to the revenue of the country. That we are all aware of and that we are all proud of, and if there is one portion of our population which ought to be proud of it more than another it is the people of British Columbia themselves. It must be admitted that man for man the people of British Columbia contribute more to our revenue than the people of any other portion of Canada, and it is very much to their credit. *It shows that they are an enterprising people and a wealthy people, and that they are not the long suffering people which the hon. gentleman from Victoria would make them out to be.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: But it is bleeding us white.
I am happy to think that if my hon. friend (Hon. Mr Prior) is a fair sample of the people of British Columbia, he is not doing justice to the people of his province.
Hear, hear.
The main grievance which the people of British Columbia have to suffer-it is a grievance which we have heard a good deal of in this House for the last fifteen years-is the Mongolian immigration.
Hear, hear.

It is not a new subject, but the hon. gentleman has presented) it to us in a new form to-day. I have followed the hon. gentleman's words very carefully and I have concluded from them that the Mongolian immigration is not altogether an unmixed evil. There appear to be some redeeming features in it. Did not my hon. friend tell us that there were 500 Celestials on board one of the Pacific steamers which recently arrived in British Columbia, and of these 500 Chinamen, 250 would remain in British Columbia and 250 would be distributed over the United States and Mexico. The hon. gentleman would lead us to believe, in other words, that the people of British Columbia import Chinamen and export them again. They, in fact, trade in Chinamen. Instead of importing horses and cattle and things of that kind they import Chinamen, keeping what they want for their own consumption and distributing the rest to the United States and Mexico.
Hear, hear.

There appears to be some profit in the trade. At all events if the people of British Columbia do not themselves derive any profit from that trade, it is clear that the steamers plying between British Columbia and China are deriving a good deal of profit. I am sure
the hon. gentleman wishes well to that line of steamers and that he would be the first to lament any conditions which would compel these steamers to give up their present trade altogether. The people of British Columbia would be sad if some day they were to find the harbour of Vancouver, which is now made glad and merry by this class of steamers, deserted by them. I do not know how far this celestial immigration may affect the trade of the line of steamers now plying between British Columbia and China, but, as my hon. friend knows, this is a problem which is now undergoing investigation, and the government are not prepared at this moment to offer any suggestion as to what policy we should apply to that long vexed problem. My hon. friend suggests that the capitation tax of $100 which we imposed last year on Chinamen coming into Canada is not sufficient, and he advocates Increasing it to $500 and imposing it not only upon Chinamen, but upon Japanese as well. I must repeat to my hon. friend that, whatever may be the report of the commission which is now investigating the question of Oriental immigration into British Columbia and therefore into Canada, we must insist at this moment, so that there may be no misunderstanding at a future date, on drawing a line between Chinese and Japanese, and that whatever policy of restriction we may adopt against Chinamen, whether it be right or wrong, we cannot afford, for the sake of Imperial policy, to treat the Japanese as we have been' treating the Chinese. The last time I had the honour to speak on this question, last session, I pointed out to my hon. friend and to the other hon. members from British Columbia, who were in the House at that time, that the possible complications which might arise at any moment in the Orient made it a matter of Imperial policy, in which Canadians should take part as well as British subjects in England, that it was of supreme importance that Great Britain should maintain friendly relations with the Emperor of Japan, and that for this reason we could not afford to treat the Japanese as we have been treating the Chinese, by restricting their immigration into Canada. I do not say that we should encourage Japanese immigration; but I certainly insist on this, which I am sure will be shared by my hon. friend, for the sake of the Imperial considerations which I have alluded to in previous sessions, and which apply to-day with greater force than I did at that time; because the complications which have arisen in China make the friendship of Japan a matter of supreme importance to Great Britain. Therefore, whatever may be the feelings of the people of British Columbia with regard to Japanese immigration, though it is not much more popular among them than Chinese immigration, still I would ask them, for the sake of the Imperial considerations which I have men-

tioned, to bear with the fact, and not attempt to force on the government of Canada the same Ideas with respect to the Japanese which prevail there with respect to the Chinese.
My hon. friend was more happy, if he will permit me to use this language, when he came to speak of the disposition of the poll tax which we levy on Chinamen. For several years past it has ranged in the neighbourhood of $200,000 a year, of which sum we have been in the habit of paying one-fourth to the government of British Columbia. The government realize that that proportion is not perhaps absolutely fair, and they propose before the 1st of July to revise and increase it. I am not prepared to say to what extent we should go. I am not prepared for one to say that we shall adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend and reverse the figures, keeping one-fourth of the amount and paying three-fourths to British Columbia, although his desire is that we should give the whole of it to that province. My hon. friend has made some comparisons between this money and the money we pay to the fishermen of the maritime provinces; but there is no comparison whatever between the two things. The idea at the basis of the payments made to the fishermen of the maritime provinces is that at a certain time during the existence of the Washington treaty the individual fishermen were deprived of their share in the fisheries, and we received $5,000,000 as a compensation for their loss The government of that day came to the conclusion that this money should be paid to the fishermen Individually who had suffered the loss, and it is being paid, not to the government of Quebec, or of Nova Scotia, or of New Brunswick, or of Prince Edward Island, but in individual payments to the fishermen themselves.
. My llon- friend has alluded to another subject as to which I must say, speaking for myself individually, and not' presuming to speak as the head of the government, that I feel a good deal of sympathy with him, that is to say, the Question of railway subsidies. My hon. friend has made a point,
I think, in favour of having another railway constructed from the coast to the mining centres of British Columbia in the Kootenay district. For my part, speaking individually, from the general observation, and not expressing any policy on behalf of the government, it seems to me only fair that the great and growing cities of the coast should have direct communication with the mining centres of British Columbia. At present they have a very inadequate communication by way of the Canadian Pacific Railway to Revelstoke and the lakes. My hon. friend has advocated the claims of the Victoria, Vancouver and Eastern Railway. I am not prepared at the present time to say that the government should subsidize this line or the other

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
line of railway. I simply take the ground that we should be guided in our policy in that respect by the consideration that we should give communication to the growing cities of the coast, Vancouver and Victoria, with the Kootenay district, the boundary district, and the other mining centres of British Columbia; and the government at the proper time, notwithstanding the advice given by my hon. friend from Toronto that we should put an end to railway subsidies, will consider that question.
1 am not prepared to express any opinion with regard to the Wellington and Cape Scott road, which is an island railway. That is a project which has some merit in it as it has been developed to me; but it does not seem to me to be of the same immediate necessity as the other roads to which I have alluded. I would say the same with regard to the Ashcroft and Cariboo district.
My hon. friend has advocated the construction of a road from Kitmat to the Yukon. With this I have absolute sympathy with my hon. friend, and he must regret the vote which he was induced to give three years ago when we introduced the policy of building a railway through Canadian territory to the waters of the Yukon. If the project which was then introduced, had been carried out, of building a railway from the Stikine river to the waters of the Yukon, which was the first link of the very railway the hon. gentleman now advocates, extending it afterwards to Kitmat Harbour and the Yukon river, the very thing my hon. friend now advocates would be to-day an accomplished fact.

Does the right hon.
gentleman say that I must regret the vote I gave ? I did not vote against it.
Did you vote for it ?
No, I was not here.
Then my hon. friend, I understand, regrets the vote he did not give.
No, I said before I left the House, that if I were here I would have voted for it.
I had forgotten that fact, and therefore apologize to my hon. friend, but let me say that the remark I made, which must not apply to him, applies merely to those around him.
Not all.

I am glad to see that there are two just on the other side. The conditions, as I have said, are no longer the same as they were. Unfortunately there is a railway now applying, running from what is American territory-but which, in my judgment, should be Canadian

territory, but which, at all events, is American territory under American control-to the waters of the Yukon. And the large trade between Seattle and the gold producing region of Canada is due largely to the establishment of that railway. But if our policy had prevailed, it is probable that the $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 a year, which now goes to Seattle, would go to British Columbia. The conditions, however, are reversed, and it is a question whether or not at present, there being a railway established and running between Skagway and the waters of the Yukon, it would be prudent to subsidize another line to the waters of the Yukon. I do not despair of having some time or other an all-Canadian route to communicate with the waters of the Yukon and Dawson City. If the scheme of my hon. friend should prove a feasible one, the government would be only too happy to give it very serious consideration, but unfortunately the action of the Senate has thrown a very serious obstacle in the way of that most laudible object.

I have been watching for some time for some hon. members from British Columbia to come to the support of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Prior), and I would just like to say a word with reference to British Columbia myself. I would wish to impress on the ministers the fact that in the eastern part of Ontario we are doing very considerable trade with British Columbia, and perhaps the House will be surprised to learn the volume of transactions that take place between us. Let me give you one illustration. Not long ago a car-load of shingles came to our town-a town in the Ottawa Valley which boasts of being the centre of the finest pine producing country in that valley-and was laid down safely in the town of Renfrew. They were the finest shingles I ever saw, and were sold to us cheaper than we could buy them at our own factories at our own door. I had some of them put on my own buildings, and never saw the like of them in my life. You would hardly think it possible that they would send from British Columbia to Renfrew shingles of such a quality, which could compete with the product of our own mills.
Then to give an illustration of our export trade to that province, during the winter season we could send them more butter than we are able to manufacture in our creamery, and in Renfrew we have one of the largest, best equipped and finest creameries on the continent. Furthermore, we fattened large quantities of poultry with the expectation of sending them to the home market in Great Britain. But to our surprise, such a demand came from British Columbia that every fowl we could lay our hands on was shipped to that province. And at the bottom of the orders were these
words: Send us the largest and finest poultry you can get. Let me add, Mr. Speaker, that although we have been dealing with British Columbia many years we never yet sent the people there a dollar's worth of goods for which we were not paid in ample time, and I cannot say that of other parts of the Dominion with which we have traded.
There is just one idea which I wish to suggest to the hon. members from that province. I notice in a paper which has just come to my hand that the project is started in Calgary of organizing an excursion of all the members of this House to the west. And if it could be arranged for us to go as far as Calgary, why should not the British Columbia representatives have it arranged that we should go as far as that province, and let us see the people out there. We are always glad to meet the representatives of that province, and the sooner we get to know the people with whom we are trading, the better it will be for all of us.

There are just one or two observations of the right hon. the leader of the government to which I would like to take exception. He spoke of the enormous loss which, he says, Canada has sustained by reason of a certain vote of the Senate. Well, if all the tales be true, a good many of the right hon. gentleman's supporters, who voted with him, went around to the Senate afterwards for the purpose of having that very measure defeated. I might also mention that a proposition to build that same railway for one-quarter the amount required by the gentleman, to whom the government proposed to give the charter, was rejected by this government, and further the proposition of a company, which desired to build the railway without any subsidy at all, was declined by the hon. gentleman and his government.
The right hon. gentleman has entirely misunderstood the observations of my hon. friend from British Columbia (Hon. Mr. Prior). My hon. friend did not suggest that this gold had been taken to Seattle because there was no railway to the Canadian seaboard, but because there is no assay office in British Columbia, and when the right hon. gentleman suggests that this gold would have gone to British Columbia, if there had been a Canadian railway, he takes an entirely incorrect view of the facts and of the observations made by my hon. friend from Victoria.
I do not intend to deal with the general observations which the right hon. gentleman made with regard to the province of British Columbia, further than that it was not correct to state that the hon. member for Toronto said there should be no more railway subsidies. He said nothing of the kind. What he said was that in the more settled portions, where we might expect traffic which would support a railway, the

policy might be adopted here, which has been adopted in the United States, namely, that these railways should be built by companies as commercial enterprises. But he did not say that in districts where it will be impossible for a long time to come that such railways could be built, this government should not assist them. And my right hon. friend's own organ, or the organ of hon. gentlemen very close to him, came out with a leading editorial, only two or three days ago, after the speech made by the hon. member for Toronto, advocating not only the same thing but going even further.
I do not desire to enter into a general discussion beyond saying that we cannot but admire the very vigorous way in which the hon. member for Victoria has put forward the claims of his province. I am not prepared, however, to accept all the comparisons he has made between British Columbia and Nova Scotia, without further investigation. Pai'ticularly is that the case with regard to the customs duties. All my colleagues in Nova Scotia know very well that a very large part of the customs duties paid by that province are paid at Montreal instead of at Halifax, and therefore the comparison made by my hon. friend in that respect is not correct.

I am afraid that somebody has been guying the hon. gentleman with respect to the proposition made a few years ago for the construction of a railway from Dawson City to the British Canadian seaboard, through British territory. The hon. gentleman gives us to understand that he received an intimation that some of those who voted for the proposition, afterwards went and sought to have it defeated. I venture to say that the hon. gentleman has been guyed in that respect. He could not find anybody on this side of the House who supported the proposition here and who asked anybody to defeat it in the Senate. I think the observations made by the leader of the House in that regard are approved by every thinking man in the House
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

speechtext:
No, no.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES-now that they have had time to reflect, free from party passion. The hon. gentleman knows well that the offer made by this government was not to pay any subsidy in cash, but to give a certain amount of what were supposed to be goldbearing lands. And he knows that these lands pictured to be of such enormous value by hon. gentlemen on that side, lie there undeveloped and unused to this day. Many hundreds of millions were to flow into the coffers of the Mackenzie & Mann from these lands which the government were placing at their disposal. These lands could Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
have been developed by hon. gentlemen opposite if they had chosen to go to work upon them. But, the lands are lying undeveloped to this day, and the country is without the all-Canadian railway which it would have had if the policy of the government had been adopted. After that policy had been submitted to the House, there was what was called the fakir proposition, submitted by a gentleman by the name of Smith, I think, who came from San Francisco-who had been exploiting the resources of the United States, and who offered to build the line for, if I remember well, one-third or one-fourth less land subsidy than that offered to Mackenzie & Mann. Nobody took that proposition seriously. There is not a man in this House who thought that the man who made it intended it to be taken seriously. As to the other proposition to which my hon. friend refers, which he says was made subsequently, to build the line without a subsidy at all. I, as one member of the government, never heard of it. I did hear of a proposition to build to an American port. But, the kernel of the proposition submitted to the government was the construction of an all-Canadian railway ending in a British port.
The Stikine was not an all-Canadian route.
Yes, it was.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It involved landing at an American port.
Why, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) says that the Stikine proposition was not to build an all-Canadian railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Decidedly ; I say that.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. The hon. gentleman must surely have forgotten the facts.

No, I remember the hon. gentleman's leader saying that we would have to negotiate with the Americans.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Why, the very gist of the proposition was to construct through British territory-not one part of the line impinged upon American territory, and a part of the proposition was to continue to a port in British Columbia.

How was the hon. gentleman going to reach that railway through British territory ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. By going up the Stikine river.
And passing through the American customs ?
Passing through by grace of the United States.
No, it was not by any grace of the United States. We had treaty rights for the navigation of the Stikine river.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The same as the Americans have on the St. Lawrence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
And, in the exercise of these treaty rights, we would reach the point where the proposed railway would cross the Stikine river. And at no place from its leaving Dawson till it reached a port on the Pacific Ocean, did that railway impinge on American territory. It was an all-Canadian line. As to the other proposition the hon. gentleman refers to, there was a proposition to build a line to an American port on the Lynn canal without a subsidy. I dare say that was what he referred to, but I do not know the particulars of it. But, there never was a proposition to build without a subsidy such a road as was proposed by this government.
My hon. friend made a few remarks with reference to the fisheries. In reply I would say a word. My hon. friend thought he was in duty bound to present here the views of a large number of those whom he represents. I watched carefully to see whether he presented those views to endorse them, but I did not gather that he desired to endorse them-he desired that they should be put on record as the views of a certain portion of the constituency he represents. He intimated that something more should be done with regard to the building of hatcheries in British Columbia, and, to show, that he had good grounds for his demands, he pointed to the action of the authorities in the adjoining state of Washington. But, I need not tell the hon. gentleman that the state of Washington, by the improvident and reckless manner in which they allowed the fisheries to be carried on, almost destroyed the salmon fisheries in their beautiful river, the Columbia, and that they are now trying to restock the river which was destroyed by the reckless fishing and the entire absence of regulation. They require, therefore, a very large number of hatcheries, and I believe that it will be many years before these hatcheries will be able, if they ever do, to bring the fisheries to the point at which they were before this wasteful and indiscriminate fishing brought it to its present condition. So far as the hatcheries in British Columbia are concerned, there is not the same necessity for them. The fish propagate themselves naturally in the Fraser river, which is their natural spawning ground ; and, up to the present
time, there is no indication of a falling off in the fishery. However, I can assure my hon. friend that the matter has not escaped our attention. We are now building a hatchery at Sicamous, and we will build one on the Skeena river, and if necessary, one at the River's Inlet. We recognize fully that we must not be niggardly in the treatment of this important industry of fishing in British Columbia. We have not been idle in the matter, but have been doing what is necessary, and we are prepared to act generously for the maintenance of the industry. The hon. gentleman referred to the protection of the fisheries in the Straits of Hecate. So far as we have territorial fisheries in these waters, I do not think the hon. gentleman can use too strong language in urging the proper and efficient protection of them. But, I think there is a misunderstanding in the minds of some of our British Columbia fellow-citizens as to where our rights begin and end. I am not going to define them or to use language which may be used hereafter to the prejudice of our claims ; but, I think very extensive claims are made. My hon. friend and I have talked the matter over, and I have pointed out that many of our friends in British Columbia imagine that we have extensive rights of fisheries which, I am somewhat afraid, may be held to belong to the nations generally, and not to the nation near whose shores the fisheries are. Now, with respect to the important question of the trap nets for the capture of salmon in British Columbia waters, I think the hon. gentleman acted wisely in not giving his approval to the proposal that these trap nets should be licensed. We have in the salmon fisheries of British Columbia a most valuable industry. I think I am correct in saying that its receipts last year were in the neighbourhood of five or six millions of dollars, all told. It is desirable that an industry that brings in such a large amount of money yearly to the people of the province should be properly preserved, not only for the present time, but for all time. The hon. gentleman speaks of the Americans catching our fish on their way through their waters. But, when you come to look at the facts, you find that the fish he speaks of as being caught by the Americans in trap nets, which they authorize from their shores, are fish coming in from the sea into American waters, and are caught on their way from the sea in American waters up to the Fraser river to spawn. Now, since they spawn on the Fraser river, they may be called ours, but they are free-swimming fish going up to spawn.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But, they were spawned in the Fraser river, for salmon go back to their own river to spawn.

But, while they are free-swimming fish, passing through American

territory, we have no ground of complaint as to their catching them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman tell me whether there have been negotiations with the United States government with a view to preserving these fish, which are likely to be exterminated altogether by the use of this device ?

I may say to my hon. friend that the negotiations on this subject formed part of the negotiations of the Joint High Commission, and they had reached a very advanced stage, and had it not been for the Alaska boundary trouble which intervened and prevented a settlement, they would have been satisfactory to both parties, because we had practically agreed upon terms which I think would satisfy both parties, international regulations which would have prevented the improper destruction of the fish. Now, let us see exactly what is desired and what is the kind of fishing that is complained of. These fish are caught in traps, very destructive, it is true. The fish go in schools through the American waters, where they are caught in these traps. From the nature of the remarks made by the hon. gentleman, one would suppose that they catch nearly all the fish taken in British Columbia waters. Such is not the fact. The hon. gentleman referred to the fact that the species of fish which is most productive, and most valuable, and brings the most'' money, is the sockeye. The hon. gentleman remarked that the Americans caught in these trap nets last year 497,000 cases of fish. Very well ; but he did not tell us what we caught by the use of our methods of fishing. I quote from the report of the fishing inspector of that province, dated January, 1900 :
In British Columbia the pack of salmon was 765,519 cases, 36,074,912 pounds, showing a satisfactory increase over that of the previous year. The total quantity of the salmon packed, 664,355 cases, were sockeyes.
So the hon. gentleman sees that in the whole province of British Columbia were packed 664,000 cases, sockeyes, all told. Now, on the Fraser river alone, I think, the pack was about 530,000 cases, as against 497,000 which the Americans packed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Were those 530,000 cases on the Fraser sockeyes altogether ?

Yes. The hon. gentleman knows that of the American pack, 245,000 cases were humpbacks. Now, the humpback is a coarse kind of fish, not of the pink, delicate colour of the sockeye, and cannot be sold in England at all,, and finds its market in the United States. All through the western United States the humpback is sold in large quantities, but we have not got access to those markets, because we
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
are met with prohibitive duties. But there is a very large undeveloped market in Japan, in China, and eastern countries, and our fishermen in British Columbia are exploiting that market now, and I have no doubt will exploit it successfully. But, keeping to this point, when we speak of salmon, we speak of the sockeye, because that is the only fish that can find a market in Great Britain. It is a fish of a very delicate flavour, and of a delicate pink complexion, and it alone will be bought by the English people. I want to point out to the hon. gentleman that there is no evidence of any failure at all on the part of our fishermen in the catch of this species of fish. It may be, and is very annoying to see their neighbours catching fish in the manner in which they do by their trap nets, while our men are prohibited from using them. But let us look at the facts. There are two or three channels leading from the San Juan de Fuca Strait, into the mouth of the Fraser river, and the fish pass through those channels, which are broad channels, and are kept free from obstructions. Our aim is to get as many fish as we can up the Fraser river. They remain for some weeks at the mouth of the river before they go up to spawn, and there they are caught by gill nets. If we allow obstructions in the shape of trap nets to be placed in the channels leading up to the British waters from the San Juan de Fuca Straits, I fear the result would be very destructive to our salmon-fishing industry. My experts advised strongly against it for years. The hon. gentleman knows that in a matter of this kind every minister must be more or less guided by the opinion of his experts, especially when these opinions coinicde with what appears to be common sense. It is undesirable to allow trap nets when the fish appear in Canadian waters. If you did so, the effect might be the destruction of the entire industry, turning the fish altogether away from the Fraser river. As it is now, we are able not only to compete with the Americans, but to hold our own fairly well, as the figures I have given the hon. gentleman show that we have held our own fairly well, athough trap nets are not allowed in our waters while they are allowed in the waters of the state of Washington. My own judgment, after talking the matter over at great length with the canners who pressed for the liberty to fish with trap nets, was against permitting their use. That judgment was based, I frankly say, to a large extent upon the advice I received from expert officers, and I think, considering that we are doing as well as we are, and that the catch continues to be as good as the figures I have quoted show, we can very well, for some years, at any rate, go along the lines we have consistently followed for years back, preserving that great industry from destruction by not allowing any destructive engine to be used in catching the sockeye. The

United States fishermen have one mode of catching fish, which is by this trap net, and we have another mode. The hon. gentleman knows that when the fish have reached the mouth of the Fraser river, and before proceeding up the river, they stay there and disport themselves around in a circle of fifteen or twenty miles, for weeks and weeks. This is the time during which our people catch these fish in gill nets, which they are there permitted to use. The Americans cannot catch them there, they are in our own waters, they do not remain in American waters for any length of time. They can only be caught by trap nets in American waters, and in no other way, because they are simpiy passing through as swiftly as they can, and if they do not catch them by trap nets they do not catch them at all. Therefore, there is ground, perhaps, for the Americans persisting in the use of trap nets, while there would be no such justification for our using them, inasmuch as we can catch them by a less destructive method, and catch them in quantities which show we can more than fairly hold our own. I know myself that a very large number of those who are best able to advise, even in British Columbia, advise that we should go very slow as regards the introduction of these trap nets. X am satisfied that my hon. friend, not being able to give any strong opinion of his own, and having placed before the House the views of a portion of his constituents, will be satisfied with the explanations which X have given.

The hon. minister of Marine and Fisheries must have a very expansive imagination. It is very evident that the proposition in regard to a railway to the. Yukon made by this government some three years ago, was an improvident one, and was an extravagant one. That was made clear to this House. But the thing made most clear to this House and the country was that their proposition was not for an all-Canadian route, but a route that was dependent entirely on the United States, on these very people that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has just said have a boundary in Alaska between us and them. The Joint High Commission failed to settle the boundary question, as the hon. gentleman says, and it is an open question to-day. This government cannot settle it, and the Americans intend to use their position on the boundary question in order to stop this railway of ours. We could not have built that railway, we could not have got into that country, we could not have taken freight off our own ships and put it on a railway, except by grace of the United States.
Nonsense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Every one knows that the one thing made clear was that it was not a Canadian route, that we were going
to be dependent on the Americans to get into that country.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that there is any contention as to where Glenora is ? There is no dispute as to the boundary there.

The right hon. gentleman is very clear in contending that the proposition laid before the House was an all-Candian proposition, but it was dependent upon the United States. That has been made perfectly clear. It is on the records. I can find speeches of the right hon. gentleman admitting that we had to get a favour from the United States in order to carry out the problem. We all know that there was to be an arrangement at Fort Wrangel, the lighting of ships at Fort Wran-gel and arranging with the United States customs officials there.
A great deal of other nonsense was talked too.
Yes, and some of it was very effective.
It killed the Bill.

And it proved that the people of Canada have a most valuable protection in the Senate. By the action of the Canadian Senate in protecting the rights of the people in regard to that proposal and in protecting the rights of the people in connection with the redistribution measure they have justified themselves for three generations to come.
And they have transferred the trade of the Yukon to Skagwny.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And turned it over to the United States.

No, they have not. If hon. gentlemen think that the trade of Canada is being turned away there is a means of keeping it. Instead of the hon. minister despairing at the situation because he did not carry out that little) tram road, it is still open to him to build a railway and it is not for him to despair because an improvident scheme happened to be defeated three years ago by the Canadian Senate. There is a way of getting into that country and of securing the trade that is done there ; let hon. gentlemen come forward now with a proposition and' it will receive fair consideration from this House. But, it must be a proposition that will commend itself to the judgment of the people. This proposition to which I have referred did not commend itself to the people because it was improvident.
Another thing that has come up in this debate, and I am glad that the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Hon. Mr. Prior) brought it up, is in connection with the ship-building

industry in this country. I believe that a broad liberal policy ought to be adopted by parliament and by the government for the establishment of the industry of ship-building. Whether it be wooden ships on the Pacific, or steel ships on the Atlantic, such a policy, I believe, will commend itself to the people of Canada. Our trade is now about to expand to an enormous degree. I believe our trade with the Pacific, in a very short time, will be as large as our trade with the Atlantic, and if this is the case we cannot too soon begin to consider how we can encourage the building of ships on the Atlantic coast and on the Pacific coast as well. I hope the day will shortly come when we will follow the example of the United States which has passed a subsidy Bill in favour of American-built ships. I hope we will do something of the same kind in order to establish that industry in Canada. If we have the iron industry developed in this country steel ship-building is its natural complement. We want to have both.
In regard to Chinese immigration we have heard a great deal about it. I have only this to say in regard to men who come from British Columbia and denounce the immigration of Chinese, that I find they have two opinions. They have a private opinion and when they come east they tell us : We cannot get along without the Chinese in British Columbia. I met a prominent newspaper man from there not long ago who has been writing in his newspaper about the curse of Chinese immigration. I asked him to tell me about that question, and he told me the public facts of it, but, he said : I do not know how I could get along in my house without Chinese servants. People from British Columbia say that there is a great deal of work which can only be done by Chinamen. They must have a straight story when they come here, and if Chinese immigration is a curse and an evil, as I believe it is, some way must be found to wipe it out, but, the people of British Columbia who talk against Chinese immigration must be prepared to forego the use of Chinese, not only in their own homes, but in connection with their works.
In connection with the establishment of the mint, I am glad to hear that another movement in the line of the national policy is to be made, namely, the establishment of a mint in this country. I happen to have in my hand a letter which I got only yesterday from a prominent firm in the; city of Toronto who said that they had considerable shipments of gold sent to them from the west and that they had trouble in realizing the full value of it. They had to pay express charges and exchange on the money coming back, but they would not have that to pay if we had a mint in this country. There is also a statement in that letter bearing out what the hon. member for Victoria says, namely, that by reason of Can-Mr. MACLEAN.
ada not having a mint, a large amount of gold and of trade goes to American cities that should be coming to Canada and which, if we had a mint, would come to Canada, and not because we have not got the Yukon railway.

I only propose to detain the House for a minute or two, and I shall not allude to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Prior). It seems to me to be somewhat regrettable that the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) should have chosen this as an opportunity to seek to justify the transaction on the part of the government in connection with the Yukon railway and to find fault with the action of the Senate of Canada in having defeated that measure. I think that the Prime Minister did not adopt that usual course of fairness that belongs to him. The right hon. gentleman, in somewhat vague terms, and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies), in bolder terms, declared that this was a OBritish-Canadian railway.
' Hear, hear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Now, the memory of the House and of the country is not so short that they will forget what constituted this British-Canadian railway. When I say 'railway,' I must apologize for having used a false term, because it was to be a tramway, 150 miles long, having no important point to start from and none to conclude at. In what manner was the balance of the route at the end of the tramway to be traversed ? It was to go through a series of rivers and lakes to reach Dawson City that are frozen up for six months in the year, while the part that is not frozen is not navigable for want of water. Yet, this is called a British-Canadian railway. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, before he sat down, declared that it was the intention of this government to build that railway from a Canadian port finally, and yet it was described as being a British-Canadian! railway. When he was asked if it would be an entirely Canadian route he said : Well, we have treaty rights. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that treaty rights are worth very little, that they are only valuable so long as the parties to the treaty are prepared to observe these rights. When the road referred to by the leader of the opposition, was brought to the attention of the House, it was pointed out that it would be met with the same difficulties, that it would depend on treaty rights that the road would be built from Skagway we would have to go through American territory, as it is claimed by the United States, but not admitted by Canada. But, hon. gentlemen forget that we are not paying one dollar out of the public purse for the building of that railway, but that the persons who built it did

so out of their own money, they took their own risk and the Dominion of Canada was in no sense involved. I think the hon. gentlemen ought to let sleeping dogs lie. In consideration of the building of this trifling tramway to provide communication with that country hon. gentlemen proposed that the whole country should he blanketed by rights given to the parties undertaking to build that railway. It is not an answer to say that these mineral lands have not been developed. If they have not been developed and if there are minerals in them Canada will still have the value of them in the future. I think hon. gentlemen will not go so far in connection with this matter as to declare in broad terms that a little tramway built into that country was to be a British-Canadian railway.
It is surely unnecessary at this time of the day to revive the question of the Stikine and Yukon Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Is that intended for the right hon. the Prime Minister ?

By no means. The right hon. the Prime Minister was led to refer to it because he was justified in believing that the existing conditions of which the hon. member for Victoria complained, were largely due to the fact that the policy which this government presented three years ago had not been approved by parliament; approval being withheld because of the determined opposition of gentlemen opposite. Why does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) persist in referring to that proposed railway as a trivial tramway, when he knows that the railway running between Skagway and Bennett and extending beyond to the River Yukon, is a narrow gauge railway of precisely the same character and description as the railway which we proposed to build ? If you speak of one in contemptuous terms you must speak in the same terms of the present railway which is doing an enormous business from the port of Skagway; a business which largely ought to be done through Canadian territory. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) knows that the object of the government was to provide at the earliest possible moment a means for the transport of mot only ordinary freight, but of supplies for our military and police forces before the close of the fall of that year. The hon. gentleman knows that the government determined upon its policy of selecting that route; first, because it was a part of an all-Canadian line; next, because it was capable of being extended, as was contemplated, to Kitmat or some desirable seaport point, although we could not complete the whole undertaking during that year. We selected the Stikine river route which runs almost entirely through our own territory. A few miles
from its mouth it runs through what the Americans claim to be their territory, but they have not even set up a claim to the river further inland, and from Telegraph Creek or Glenora where our railway would have started, the territory was ours without any dispute. In order to avail of the quickest and speediest way of getting into that country, we had to utilize the Stikine river.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not a fact that at that time the limited States authorities had a custom-house at Fort Wrangle ?

No doubt they had, and why ? Because the Stikine river passer for a short distance through territory which they claim to be theirs, and at Fort Wrangle situated on the mouth of the river there is a custom port. But that would not militate in the slightest degree against our free and uninterrupted use of that channel as a means of getting to our own territory, when hon. gentlemen say that we would be prevented from passing Fort Wrangle, and going up the Stikine river it is equivalent to saying that the United States government without any reason in the world would take up an attitude of hostility and precipitate war between the Imperial government and themselves. They could not violate that treaty without confronting a declaration of war. The Imperial government could not countenance such a thing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the minister say that the Americans could not harass us with regulations that would make it worthless.

I say unquestionably no. There are other points where they have to pass Canadian custom-houses, and there are points where we have to pass American custom ports, and there is no difficulty in the world.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At Skagway ?

Yes, at Skagway, as my right lion, friend suggests. At Skagway it is done to-day. Have we any trouble at Skagway ? Is there any difficulty in getting our shipments through that point ? None whatever. The United States government have afforded us every facility. They have treated us as they would he bound to treat us at all times when we are in friendly relations with them, as I hope we ever shall be. They have treated us fairly as ithey would expect to be treated fairly by us. The most serious obstacle that could arise at Skagway would be that our ships in jmssing would have to report, or that we would have to report a transfer from larger to smaller craft. All they would do would he possibly to put an officer on our vessels to see that we would not land goods on their territory and thus escape the

payment of duties on goods which are subject to duty. But the moment we went beyond the admitted boundaries between the two countries they would no longer have control and they would no longer have one of their officers in charge. There would be no obstacle whatever, but even if we should have had to face some obstacles, which I believe we would not, would it not be worth while to try it for the purpose of securing an immediate means of getting into our own country over our own territory and by a railway of our own. Was it not all the more reason why we should try the experiment, seeing that this was only going to be a temporary arrangement, and seeing that the proposition that the government laid before parliament involved an early extension of this line of railway from Glenora to Kitmat or any other port we should select which would unquestionably be in our own territory. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) knows perfectly well that last session or the session before, his ex-leader (Sir Charles Tupper) declared in parliament that it was a matter of extreme regret that that line of railway had not been constructed, and he attributed the serious disaster to one of the companies with which he was associated, to the fact that that railway was not in existence. Why is it that hon. gentlemen opposite will persist to endeavour to create an erroneous impression in regard to this ? Why is it that they persist in creating the impression that we would not have had an adequate and complete line of railway over our own territory exclusively, and entirely, if we had been permitted to carry out the policy which we laid before parliament then ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Intercolonial Railway-Strengthening bridges,

We are asking parliament to give us a further sum this year of $100,000 for strengthening bridges on the Intercolonial Railway. On a former occasion I explained that this vote was being asked for in order that we might have our bridges made of sufficient strength and capacity to carry the heavy locomotives and the heavy trains which must pass over them. We are proposing to expend in this way $100,000 this year. I could give hon. gentlemen who are interested in it a statement of the particular bridges we have in view this year, if it is desired.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it would be desirable for us to know what the bridges are, and whether they are to be rebuilt or merely strengthened.

Perhaps my hon. friend did not follow my explanation of this matter last session. The bridges on the Intercolonial Mr. BLAIR.
are almost entirely of a uniform span. There may be two different classifications of spans, but there are not a great variety of them. This is a very fortunate circumstance, because it enables us to double the strength of a bridge at one point by taking a span from a bridge at another point and placing two spans together. This necessitates the placing of a new span at the point from which a span has been removed. These bridges are in a thoroughly good condition in every respect; they are the bridges which were put on the line at the time of its original construction, and would last for probably a century more; but we have adopted the present policy because the bridges require to be made heavier and stronger. These changes are to take place at Middle River, Nash's Creek, Sayabec, Grant's Brook, Nigado New Mills, McKinnon's Brook, Grand Bie, Grenville, Eel River, Mill Creek, Gilmour's Creek, Little Metis River, Louison Brook, and Clark's Brook.

speechtext: I see that this was paid by virtue of an order in council of the 15th of October, 1900. That certainly seems a very high price, and I would like some information as to how the government arrived at this value.

There can be no doubt, from the information in possession of the department that the prices at which we secured these lots from the heirs of Rhodes and the heirs of Young were very low. The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that there is no difference between what should be paid for filled ground and for ground that is not filled, indicates that he is not acquainted with the situation there. The ground which is open to be flooded and is flooded at every rise of the tide, one would say off-hand, would not be so valuable as land which is filled in and ready for the erection of buildings immediately and upon which some buildings may have been standing at the time. The land was obtained after there had been a careful examination by our engineer, Mr. Mackenzie, upon whose advice we acted in the matter. The small piece of ground he refers to, was, I think, a triangular piece taken off another larger tract, and which we require to enable us to make a curve of our track and get on to the piece where we are going to build, and where we have built our crib-work, and on which we intend to lay the tracks and place the station. This small triangular piece of ground off the larger piece would to some extent impair the value of the ground remaining, and we would expect to have to pay the price which was asked. We have exercised the utmost care and vigilance in respect to the prices. Where there could be any doubt at all raised, we have preferred to submit the whole matter to judicial consideration and determination, although the experience of the late government and our own experience have not been encouraging in that regard. We have not found that the courts are ready to place a low valuation upon property; in fact I think we have had to pay as much, and in many cases more, than we would have had to pay by making a bargain ourselves.
