I cannot say just what property was expropriated, but I think land, taken in I.evis for the purpose of the Intercolonial Railway, was valued by the Exchequer Court and that it was valued at a price in excess of any price that we have paid here. The name of the lawyer was Mr. Lemieux.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not aware that any expropriation was made in my time for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway at L6vis.
I do not know that there was. I did not say so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that his predecessor had paid a higher price ?

When I speak of my predecessor, I mean the late government. I do not mean to say that the hon. gentleman was the individual minister. I was then enforcing the argument which I have just now repeated, that the expropriation proceedings before the Exchequer Court have not resulted to the advantage of the department and have not made us feel that this is the most desirable way, in the interests

of the exchequer at all events, to have these values fixed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Were there any expropriations at Levis made by the Exchequer Court as at present constituted ?

1 have understood that the lands that were taken for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway from Levis all the way through on the St. Charles branch were dealt with by the Exchequer Court. We know with what alarming results they were so dealt with.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I remember rightly, the Exchequer Court was appointed long since then with Mr. Burbidge as judge. There may have been the power of exchequer in the Supreme Court, and that court may have dealt with these lands, but I do not think the expropriations were made by Judge Burbidge.
My deputy tells me they were.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: 1 am informed that almost the whole ground that was taken In connection with the St. Charles branch was dealt with by the court.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You said by the Exchequer Court. If I remember rightly, the Exchequer Court is a creation since these apppropriations.

I am speaking of my own experience. Of course it must necessarily be of the Exchequer Court because there is no other tribunal that I could speak of in reference to these matters since I came into the department. I unhesitatingly say that my experience of the Exchequer Court has not been satisfactory. It is too liberal in its allowances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman give me the total quantity of land expropriated ?
I could add up the quantity stated on page 330 of ' Hansard.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that there are about a couple of acres that you are paying $110,000 for.
We are not paying any more than we can help.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you know whether Mr. Pugsley was acting for any of the owners of the property in the sale to the government ?

The only property that I know 1304
that Mr. Pugsley had any connection with at all is the property that has not been closed for, the property which we had determined to expropriate because we would not agree to pay the price asked for it. Mr. Pugsley and some other legal gentlemen have been communicating with the department and urging the payment of the amount which they claim should be paid for this land, but we have not taken this land. We have declined to pay the lowest price that w'e could get them to agree to and the probabilities are that there will be expropriation proceedings.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Do you know the land which Mr. Pugsley is acting for, aud what price is it that they demand from the government for it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. $2.10 a foot is what they are asking.

Is it the Couture property ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Yes.
To dredge and blast rock at Halifax, $20,000.
Mr.	BORDEN (Halifax). Is that for
work at Richmond ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Yes. There are some 3,000 cubic yards to remove at the deep water terminus.

The deep water terminus is nearly half a mile below the station. I have no doubt that further accommodation is required, but, as I have pointed out before, it seems to me the best way to get the facilities and room there would be by the expropriation or acquisition of property at Upper Water street.

The Water street property would be for local purposes, but this is in connection with the sea-going business. We have to dredge there to accommodate the shipping. and getting property at Water street would have no relation to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can understand that.
What is the total cost of this work to be ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has it been let by contract and tender ?
There have been $3,200 spent up to the present time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who were the contractors, and was if let by public tender ?
Beazley Bros. & Company are the contractors, and probably the leader of the opposition knows the firm. [DOT]
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do know them. I think they are very good men.
Their price was $9.75 a yard, which was settled upon after public tender.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Were they the lowest tenderers ?
The MINISTER' OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. Yes.
What depth of water will you have at the deep water terminus.
My recollection is that this was applied for by the board of trade. After they made the application it was found that there would have to be this additional blasting done.
I think that is the case. I was anxious to ascertain the depth of water after the work was completed.
I cannot state precisely, but I imagine we would get 28 feet of water at low tide. '
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I trust that when this blasting is accomplished the Minister of Railways and Canals will not be quite so forgetful of the existence of Halifax as a port in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, as he seemed to be last autumn when he was discussing certain matters with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

I will not forget Halifax, I can assure you.
Mr, BORDEN (Halifax). My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) was so forgetful of Halifax at that time, that it seemed entirely to have escaped his mind for the moment. That may happen only occasionally, but at all events when he addressed the communication to Mr. Shaughnessy he seemed to have forgotten that Halifax had certain facilities for the purpose of doing export business that would come over the Intercolonial Railway. I trust that when the Minister of Railways gets the port of Halifax into thorough working order he will not permit the Intercolonial Railway terminus at Halifax, and the port of Halifax itself, to so completely -escape from his mind as he seems to have done on that occasion.
The MINISTER' OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I shall endeavour not to forget it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Increased accommodation, St. John, N.B., $100,000.
What is this for ?

In addition to; the engine-house we have, we propose to erect a twenty-four stall new engine-house. Under our arrangement we provide accommodation at St. John for the Intercolonial Railway locomotives as well as for the Canadian Pacific Railway locomotives, and we will require the twenty-four stalls for the larger engines. The building was estimated to cost $100,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why does not the minister state the purpose of this building in the item ?
It is certainly for increased accommodation. The expression in the estimate is not an invention of mine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This would be a proper time for the minister to make an explanation in reference to what negotiations he has had with the Canadian Pacific Railway with regard to the trade of St. John.
I would not select just this moment for that purpose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like the hon. minister to lay on the Table the whole of the correspondence with the Canadian Pacific Railway in reference to making St. John a winter port, and a statement of the whole expenditure since he has been in power on the accommodation at St. John.

If there is any correspondence which has not already been brought down, I will bring it at once.
HOn. Mr. HAGGART. The sum of $100,000 seems an enormous sum for an engine house.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is a large engine house, and it includes the land.
. Hon. Mr. HAGGART. What is the estimated cost of the engine house and of the land ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This amount includes a turntable and a workshop in connection with the engine house, at a total cost of $80,000. It is estimated that the land to be acquired in connection with it will cost $20,000, making the neat $100,000. That is the form in which the figures have been given to me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where is that particular lot of land ?

It is a short distance up the line of the Intercolonial, about a mile from the

station. It is outside of the city, though the city limits may possibly include it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How many acres ?
There are six acres.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is over 83,000 an acre. There must be a boom on in St. John.
Let me draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that the Canadian Foundry Company in Toronto bought thirty acres of land, partly in the city of Toronto and partly outside of it, for $20,000.

The land has not been purchased yet. This is the estimate which has been given to me by the officers of the department, and it may be that the whole of this sum will not be required. If it is not, it will not be expended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: To my knowledge, land inside of the municipality of Montreal, in the east, very well situated, practically within the business part of the city, is being offered for about $1,500 an acre. In Toronto it is offered at less than that. In Buffalo, to my knowledge, a large block of land belonging to the Erie Railway, in the middle of the busy railway part of the town, was offered a few days ago at $1,500 an acre, and the parties *who owned the mortgage on it refused to redeem it at that price. In Toronto, the Canada Foundry Company bought land at less than $1,200 an acre. If in St. John you are paying nearly $3,500 an acre for land, there must be something wrong.
I want some verification of the statement that you can buy land in the 'heart of the city of Buffalo for $1,500 an acre.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not say in the heart of the city of Buffalo. I said in the railway part of it.
I do not think you could buy it in the railway part of any town in Canada at that price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
You can not get it in Ottawa for anything like that.
Mr* OSLER. Ottawa is the seat of government, and I do not wonder that land is dear.
Will the minister state for what purpose that land is used at present ?

I do not know the particular piece of land which is proposed to be taken. The engineer has been over the ground, and he is a very careful man, as every one knows, and has made his estimate on the
best information he could gather. Certainly we are not going to pay any more for the land than we are absolutely obliged to pay. If we cannot get it on terms which we think satisfactory, we shall have to expropriate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Who owns the land ?
I cannot say.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: All the land within a mile of the city of St. John is used for farming purposes, except what is devoted to some manufacturing businesses, which I presume the minister would not think of attempting to buy. The land along the line of the Intercolonial within several miles of the city of St. John, is used for grass land or market gardening. This would seem to be a high price to pay for that class of land.
We have not bought the land. It has not been engaged.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If you put an appropriation in your estimates of such an amount of money for six acres, it means that you hold it open to somebody to get that price for 'the land.
I do not think it at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. If you cannot get land on the outskirts of St. John City for less money, and put up a round-house, you should not put up your round-house at all until you get the land cheaper.

It is not said that we are asking $20,000 for the land alone, we are asking increased accommodation, and are asking $100,000 to cover the cost, and have given the details. The land will not be had at any higher price than we are obliged to pay. The engineer has made his estimate, and it may be that he has made a liberal estimate as to what he thinks will be the cost. It may be that his estimate is in excess of what will be required. We are not asking simply for a round-house, but we have to lay down a considerable quantity of tracks in connection with the buildings, so that we may have the necessary car accommodation and the required yard room. The city of St. John is very singularly situated in one respect. The main point of the city is built on hills, and the land on the level below the height of ground is narrow and of necessity more expensive than it would be in a city built upon a long stretch of level ground. The ground on which this yard is to be placed is very circumscribed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman the plan of the engineer of the

ground where he intends to locate the round-house ?
The plans are not prepared yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman said that he had a recommendation from his engineer who carefully went into the question.
Yes, as to the necessity of having a round-house and tracks and a yard, but the plans will not be prepared until the appropriation passes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Surely you had the plans before asking for the appropriation. That is the customary way.
The engineer says that is not the custom at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, it is time'it was. The idea of asking $100,000 for the purpose of building a round-house on the recommendation of the engineer that the round-house will cost $80,000 and the land $20,000 ! The hon. minister stated some time ago that this round-house was to be located about a mile from the city, outside St. John. Surely he has an estimate from his engineer. The engineer could not have arrived at the figure of $80,000 for the round-house and $20,000 for the land without furnishing the minister with a detailed account showing how these amounts were made up. If the minister has not that detailed account, he has no business coming here and asking for an estimate. Then the minister asks $20,000, and says the land is to be expropriated, and only a fair price paid for it. We have had money voted for the purpose of expropriating land at Point L6vis, and we have not expropriated the whole of the land required. The land required is in the neighbourhood of five acres and $100,000 is the cost.
Does the hon. gentleman say that that is beyond the valuation there ? I challenge him to prove that one dollar has been paid more than the reasonable value of the land.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If $20,000 is not an excessive value for an acre of land, or $100,000 for five acres around the station at Point LSvis. I do not know what is. The idea of a lot of land 89 feet by 100 feet with nothing on it, costing $8,900 ! I say it is an exorbitant price.
The hon. gentleman knows nothing about it. Not one farthing has been paid in excess of the value. Let anybody go to L6vis and inquire. We have been about three years quarrelling with the
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: people there in order to get the value down to the point to which we have got it. I challenge my hon. friend to make an investigation at any moment. Let him call his committee and bring witnesses, and I defy him to prove that one dollar was paid in excess of the value of the land at LSvis down to the present moment. If there should be an expropriation, of course, witnesses will be called, and they will put on a higher value. The hon. gentleman knows nothing about the subject when he states the price is excessive.

I know the value of the land as well as the hon. minister. Here is a lot of land 89 feet by 100 feet, without a building on it, situated near the station at Point L6vis, for which the hon. gentleman pays $8,950, and he is asking a vote for the purpose of paying for land, should it be required in the same neighbourhood, $2.60 per foot, when they only paid a dollar for this other land.
I have not asked for $2.60 per foot.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What the hon. gentleman does say is that Mr. Couture is asking for a lot of property in the same neighbourhood $2.60 per foot, and he thinks the amount is excessive, and proposes to refer the matter to the Exchequer Court.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Pugsley of St. John is one of the parties interested as solicitor or something else with reference to this particular land. The probability is it will never go to the Exchequer Court. However, if the hon. gentleman does refer the matter to the Exchequer Court, the judgment of that court will be fixed by the evidence produced on behalf of the government as to the value of the land, and it is often found a convenient way for a minister, who wants a justification for the amount he is paying, to let the case go to the Exchequer Court on an ex parte statement by the parties offering the land to the government.

The hon. member has been a responsible minister of the Crown, and I ask him if it is possible to carry cto the government if ministers are liable to have insinuations cast at them such as the hon. member has just thrown ? I could make allowance if the hon. gentleman were an ignoramus who had never been charged with the responsibility of a department, but to take the stand that no matter what the minister may do. whether he settles for the land without going to the Exchequer Court and proceeds by expropriation, or goes to the Exchequer Court, somebody's name may be dragged in who has something to do

with it as a friend of the government, and the whole thing is a job, no matter how the minister may proceed, is unworthy of the hon. gentleman. If the minister goes to the Exchequer Court, then he is to be charged with producing witnesses who will exaggerate the value of the land, and if he does not then he is consenting to an exorbitant price. So that whatever he does the transaction is a discreditable one. Yet the hon. gentleman who takes this course is one who at one time held the responsible position of a minister of the Crown. I say it is discreditable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I quite realize that people who have land to sell to a railway company try all they can to get an exorbitant price. If the company is forced into such a position that they must get a small piece of land, even if they pay two or three times its value-and I am speaking from an experience of twenty years in expropriating lands in the west in connection with railways-once the railway company finds that it is being held up and is asked $2,000 or $3,000 an acre for land that is only worth $100 an acre, the managers of the company, if they do their duty, should say at once: We will have nothing more to do with it. The Grand Trunk Railway put their yard four or five miles out of Toronto because they could not get land within the city at a fair price. The Canadian Pacific Railway built their yard at the junction a little outside Toronto because they could not get land at a fair price inside, and they did this with very little detriment to the operation of the road, if not to its benefit. If you make estimate anything like $20,000 an acre, quite possibly the men who own the land will ask that much, and in such case it is the duty of the government to say : We will not build our station if you are going to hold us up to that price, because there is no land there worth that. Quebec, as we know, has not had a land boom for a great many years. We have one of the ministers of "the Crown, I believe, who has conscientious scruples about the price proposed to be paid for the Plains of Abraham, a very valuable property adjoining the city of Quebec. I think he is right. And this government, managing its public railway, has no right to ask this House for any sum such as $20,000 an acre for the extension of their yard in Point Levis. Stop it, and do not build the road.

The facts are not as the gentleman (Mr. Osier) states them. I do not understand that we are paying or proposing to pay $20,000 an acre. But whatever we have paid, we have paid because we could not get the property by any means for less. It is not fair, it is not reasonable to say that the situation at Levis is the same as the situation anywhere else. Any hon. gentlemen who have gone through Levis on the Intercolonial Railway know that there is a very narrow strip between the precipice on one side and the water on the other. And, in order to widen our right of way and afford us the additional room we require we must take the land which is available. The Couture property, which has been referred to, is exceedingly valuable to this man, and the same is true of the other property we have taken. We must get through there ; we cannot do as the hon. gentleman suggests and say to the people : If you do not give us this land at a price that we think is reasonable we will not take it. We must get our road through there to meet the necessities of the traffic. If this were a spur we were throwing out or some new undertaking that did not absolutely involve the running of the railway, we could take that position-and I would be the first to take it, as I have done in several Instances. But at L6vis we must have the ground and we must agree with the people, or if we cannot agree with them if they ask an exorbitant price, our only course is to refer the matter to the court. That is what we have agreed to do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has the business in Quebec so increased, notwithstanding that you have taken the terminus to Montreal ? Has the local business so increased that you must have this land at once ? Has not Levis been relieved by taking the terminus to Montreal ?

The business at LSvis has increased. There is only a single track through Ldvis, with a fence on either side and every train, even with our immensely increased trade, must go through that congested district. It has been a reproach to the road and a delay to business. The inconvenience is increasing every day, and at any cost it can be tolerated no longer. If we cannot keep down the price to be paid for these lands by proceedings through the Exchequer Court there is no way by which we can do it. Unfortunately, we have not always succeeded in doing that in the past -I do not know that we have ever succeeded.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I might point out that the rate at which some of this land is being bought would not give $20,000 an acre but $75,000 an acre.
We bought it by the foot and we paid a reasonable price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not discussing that, I am discussing the price per acre. Another lot the hon. gentleman bought at 80 cents a square foot, which would be $25,000 an acre. If you take the average you will find that this land will cost more than $25,000 an acre.
Can the hon. gentleman tell the total amount that will have been expended on the Intercolonial Railway in St. John including these improvements ?
The total expenditure on capital account in St. John, from the beginning of the road up to the Slst December last, was $2,168,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can the hon. gen-telman give the total expenditure on capital account at Levis ?
No, I have not got that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not think there is a gentleman in this House who objects to any expenditure in St. John or its vicinity which would have the tendency to develop that port or increase the trade of Canada. But since this government came in, this government of business men, there have beeu some examples of the most lavish expenditures, I believe, ever known in this country, and I believe the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) has not been exempt from that accusation. His record began before he came to this House by leaving his province in debt some $3,000,000. The first contract which was let under him in St. John gives some little idea of the hon. gentleman's method in connection with such work. He called for tenders and received three at least which we have had brought to the notice of this House.
What work was that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: St. John harbour. One tender was from Mr. Mayes for $219,990 ; one from Mr. Heney foil $298,193, and one from Mr. Connolly for $328,173. And Mr. Connolly, the highest tenderer, obtained the contract. It is true that Mr. Mayes asked the privilege of bringing a dredge into this country free of duty. If any hon. gentleman in this House had had these three contracts submitted to him and had had the power, he would have allowed that dredge to come in free of duty. It would not have been the first instance when the country had the benefit of freedom from duty, for the Minister of Railways, during the past few years, has brought in hundreds of thousands in value of cars, engines, and other equipment for the Intercolonial Railway into the country free of duty. Had he allowed this and accepted Mr. Mayes' tender $10S.1S3 would have been saved to this country. Mr. Mayes was not in a position to be so friendly and convenient as Mr. Connolly could be. However, Mr. Mayes did receive a sub-contract, I believe, for just such portions of the work as he wanted. But it is evident that if the minister had been a business man, as he should have been, he might have saved the country $108,000. Then, I had occasion to call the attention of

the minister a few weeks ago to another little business transaction of his. He stated on the floor that the contract with Mr. Connolly would be lessened by $34,000 from the fact that he had Mr. Heney's and Mr. Mayes' deposit cheques amounting to $34,000. But, strange to say, the deposit cheques never turned up, though two years and a half have elapsed since they came in, until inquiry was put on the paper, and we found that they were pigeon-holed, I believe, with a loss to the country of $3,400 in interest. That is the sort of business methods followed by the hon. gentleman at the head of the department. An inquiry was made with regard to the shipment of grain by the hon. meipber for Lennox (Mr. Wilson). This elicited the information that 507,576 bushels had been exported from the city of St. John. Inquiry was made of the minister as to whether the grain was not carried to St. John at a loss, but he failed to get a reply. If the minister is running a railway on business principles, he knows to a dollar how much loss he made on that grain. I would like to ask the minister over what road that grain came to Montreal ?
Let the hon. gentleman go on, and I will answer him when he has finished.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand a portion came over the Parry Sound and the Canada Atlantic Railway. I understand he has some arrangement with these roads, and it is reported that the hon. gentleman purposes extending the Intercolonial Railway system to Parry Sound. Will the hon. gentleman tell me if the Intercolonal Railway has an oflice in the city of Ottawa ?
I will make a note of it, and answer the hon. gentleman by-and-by, when he gets through.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I regret to see that he shows the same culpable ignorance on this matter as on many others. But I understand that the Canada Atlantic Railway are doing the business of the Intercolonial Railway for the city of Ottawa. Now, at the eastern terminus, or termini, of the Intercolonal Railway, we have two cities, Halifax and St. John, at least we think so down in New Brunswick. But when I take up the time table of the hon. gentleman's agency in Ottawa, I find there is only one terminus, the city of Halifax. St. John is not given on the outer side of this time table at all, and I find on turning to the inside of the table there is no such place as St. John on the map. I will send this oyer to the minister, and let him find his city of St. John, if he can, on that map. Not only is it not on this time table, but you can walk down to the Russell House and see an enlarged map of this route, and you will still fail to find on it that there is any

such city in Canada as St. John, notwithstanding that the hon. gentleman is presumed to represent that city in this House. The city of St. John has spent thousands of dollars this year in arranging, through toursts' associations, to advertise the city, and here is the Minister of Railways and Canals, the representative of that city, who Will not even name the city on his map. There are several other things I might mention, showing the business management of the hon. gentleman. One of them was that beautiful contract for steel rails, and we had some suggestion made also in regard to the Kingston locomotive works, two things that were almost coincident with the election. So the hon. gentleman had all the advantages possible at the country's expense to assist his friends in the last Dominion election ; and it may be that even this contract in St. John might savour somewhat of that character, as it was made just about 'the time, I believe, of a local election in New Brunswick. There seems, at least, to be rather an odd coincidence in this case, and I believe that word ' coincidence ' will be remembered by the Minister of Railways and Canals very well, for he used it frequently in some of his arguments in New Brunswick, in a manner in which I do not think he will ever use it again. Now, if the Minister of Railways and Canals is expending this money in St. John in a reasonable way, I assure him that every member from New Brunswick will be glad to support him.. But we believe in New Brunswick that although he represents the city of St. John, he should be just as careful of the money of the people in that city as anywhere else. Judging from the way he has expended part of that money in St. John, it is necessary to scrutinize carefully the items he brings before us.
To provide additional sidings along the line.
These sidings will be required at various points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the minister was going to give an answer to my hon. friend from Charlotte (Mr. Ganong).

speechtext: I would like to have some further information. I would like to have the list, and I would like to have it before this item passes. Since the hon. gentleman has referred to some observations which I made a moment or two ago, and which he thinks are a sufficient answer to the hon. member for Charlotte, I may say to the hon. gentleman that I do not think his neglect of either St. John or Halifax is an answer to a complaint on behalf of either city. The hon. gentleman seems to think that Halifax and St. John are necessarily in antagonism to each other, and that if he can point out to my hon. friend from Charlotte that on some other occasion he has neglected Halifax in some way, and that is a complete answer to the charge that he is apparently neglecting St. John now. Surely, the hon. gentleman is forgetting the logical training of his early youth, when he attempts to make au answer of that kind to my hon. friend. The complaint which I made was this ; last autumn, the hon. gentleman was discussing with the Canadian Pacific Railway an offer which they had made to him to send over the Intercolonial Railway the whole of the traffic that had formerly gone over the Canadian Pacific Railway short line to St. John, so that, with his elevator and facilities at St. John, he could deal with it, and he gave the answer that he was not able to deal with the traffic at St. John, but he absolutely ignored Halifax. I have his letter before me, if the hon. gentleman should see fit to deny it. I have the letter in which that statement I make to the committee is fully substantiated. I do not think it is an answer to my hon. friend from Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) to say that I made a complaint. I complain of that conduct still, and it is no answer to the hon. gentleman from Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) that the hon. minister was guilty of neglect on that occasion. What is it that the hon. member for Charlotte is complaining of? It is that upon the time table in which the hon. gentleman is making close connection, you do not find the location of the harbour of St. John marked.
St. John is on this map.

I am only discussing what was put forward by the hon. member for Charlotte. I have not examined the map, I do not know whether his statement is correct or not. I say, that, although I come from the city of Halifax, I am prepared to back up the hon. member for Charlotte in any reasonable complaint he may make on behalf of the city of St. John, just as I would be prepared to back

up any complaint on behalf of the city of Halifax, and I do not think the hon. minister is treating the committee with proper respect, when he will not make answer to certain questions which the hon. member for Charlotte asks, and then has the item passed while we are expecting the information, afterwards standing up and making certain remarks which were not exactly framed in that courteous tone which we would expect from a minister of the Crown in passing his estimates.

I do not think there are very many hon. members of the House who would object to the answer that the hon. minister gave that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), had sufficiently answered the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong), when we consider the spirit in which the hon. member for Charlotte made his attack. I am not going to say much about it except that I have the time table in my hand which he referred to. I can hardly see how fairly a point can be made out of this time table which is produced. It is a Canada Atlantic time table, and it professes to be a condensed time table. On the map, St. John is marked as distinctly as Halifax is marked, one of the termini of this railway. St. John is marked there and the line of the railway is heavily marked.
Spell St. John.

S-t. J-o-h-n. An ordinary man would understand that to be St. John, N.B. The time of leaving is on the table, the time of arriving is on the table, and I do not see what more the hon. gentleman could require than that. But the time table of the Intercolonial Railway, which is the government road, and which is the road which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has charge of, has all the particulars that any hon. gentleman could require in reference to St. John. It does look as if an hon. gentleman was pretty hard up Immaterial with which to make an attack when he uses such arguments as the hon. member for Charlotte uses.

My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Britton) has to support the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals anyway. It does not make any difference. The hon. minister, when down in the small province of New Brunswick, could clap his hat on and run away if the opposition brought anything up, but here, he has to face the music although he frequently turns his back. This idea of venting spleen and bile is not a new expression. He used it in four different meetings in Charlotte, when he came down to help elect me, because, in every division, except one, in which he spoke I got increased majorities. I hope he will come back again. We will give him a warm reception. In regard to

this map, Portland, apparently the winter-port of the Intercolonial Railway, is shown in good shape, but St. John is not on the map. I asked the hon. minister on purpose to find out why it was not there. He declined, of course, to reply. He is getting back to his old New Brunswick tactics again. The minister is easily ruffled. This evening he got up to lecture the committee just as he used to do and with as little effect as in New Brunswick. When he gets up in this House it would be more becoming his position to treat hon. members with respect and to give answers in reply to questions. It is his business to do so and lie had better attend to it.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he has any plan or principle at all as to the charging of these things to capital account ? If the Intercolonial Railway had been an ordinary private corporation this capital account would have been closed long ago. In thd period of boom times, all these items the minister is now charging to capital would have been charged to revenue. Is the minister going for all time to adopt the principle of charging every new siding to capital account ? There is absolutely no end to the capital account you may roll up, because you have the credit of the government behind you to borrow all you want. There is no means of knowing how the Intercolonial Railway is paying if all these things are charged to capital account. Half of this estimate in an ordinary railway company would be charged to running expenses. Out of this three million odd dollars In the first column, at least a million and a half would be charged to revenue in an ordinary railway company.
Oh, no.

Yes, without any question. In the case of an absolutely new railway for perhaps ten years after it is completed you would add to capital account the rolling stock, increased siding and these things, but in the case of a railway completed for twenty-five years like the Intercolonial Railway, so far as these sidings and extensions to stations are concerned, its capital account is closed. The criticism would be so adverse to any private company that it could not exist if it were to charge these things to capital.

The hon. gentleman is quite in error in stating that on railways which have been in operation for twenty-five or thirty years additional sidings are charged to revenue and not to capital. The Star newspaper contains a report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in London yesterday, and there is a statement that a very large sum was spent by the Grand Trunk Railway for additional sidings, and charged to capital account. If you are going to adopt a correct system it is just as necessary to charge additional new sidings to capital as if they were built in the first instance. It is not a repair ; it is an addition. The time comes in the life of a railway as it has come in the life of the Intercolonial Railway, when it is necessary that an entire change should be made as to the weight of its locomotives, as to the size of its cars, as to the weight of its rails, as to the length of its sidings, as to the size of its engine houses, and as to a number of other things. There is a doubling up all
over the whole line, and it has to be done within a very limited time. If you are going to lay down a thousand miles or 500, or 100 miles of new sidings-not repairing or replacing the old-why should you not charge that to capital just the same as the first sidings constructed. If you are going to re-rail your line from one end to the other, of necessity you must charge the difference to capital. If you are going to increase the capacity of your road all over, why should you not charge it to capital. We hope to complete these sidings within a few years, and it would be a physical impossibility to do it out of earnings no matter what margin you might have.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose you take the old rails from the main line and put them on the sidings, how do you make your charge?

So far as these rails are used they are charged to capital according to the value of the rail as you have credited your stores account with them. You do not charge any more than that. It is utterly impossible for you to charge such a complete transformation of your railway from end to end to earnings.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I presume that the- minister is making use of the old 67-pound rails on the sidings when he replaces them by the 80-pound rails, and as there is no cost for right-of-way, the cost of ties and the labour is the only charge. That does not amount to a great deal, and it should be charged to revenue. I presume that is what the minister is doing.
I did not hear any mention of Pictou in the list of stations read out by the minister.
We are going to have something in the supplementary estimates for Pictou.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why does the minister not charge his coal bill to capital account ? It is a big amount. I do not object to the Intercolonial carrying goods free, if that is for the benefit of the country ; but let us know what it costs. Do not let us charge the repairing of platforms, the putting in of new semaphores and new lamps, * and every other miserable thing that enters into the mending of a road, to capital account, and lump them in an item of $50,000 to provide increased facilities along the line.

The hon. gentleman's statement will go to ' Hansard,' and possibly somebody may read it ; and if they do, they will read that the hon. member for West Toronto, a person of some authority, stated in the House that a vote was being asked on capital account to mend platfbrms and to repair lamps and semaphores. speechtext: Well, I will put it as it is. The hon. minister says that $240 is for extending platforms. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
A petition has been forwarded to me with respect to the position of affairs at the Strait of Canso. I do not know whether it bears on this or not; I will read it to the hon. gentleman. It seems to have been signed toy a number of residents at Guysborough, Straight of Canso :
Humbly showeth, that whereas you, the hon. Minister of Railways, have publicly announced that there will be a large sum of money expended at the Strait of Canso for the purpose of providing better wharf and dock accommodation for the new ferry steamer, which is soon to ply on the Strait of Canso to meet the requirements of the enormous increase in freight and passenger traffic to and from Cape Breton ; and, whereas, the present wharf terminus of the government railway at Mulgrave is unfortunately located in a very cramped place under the hill with the inconvenience of a back switch for the approach to and from the main line of railway, and with very limited space for the extension of further railway facilities, and with no room to make further wharf and dock room free or secure from the regular current and ice which proves so troublesome in the ferry dock now in winter.
Does the bon. gentleman recognize it ?

Yes.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)-(reading) :
Your petitioners therefore ask that you extend the main line only a few hundred yards further south to Pirate Harbour, a cove which, from its location, forms a natural terminus and direct approach to the main line of the government railway. Pirate Cove has a good depth of water, is free from sunken rocks and shoals on all sides, and also affords an excellent site for wharfs and docks sheltered from the regular current of running ice through the strait in winter, and further, has almost unlimited space for the further extension of terminal facilities which seem to he so much required in the near future.
I have not any opinion about the subject-matter of the petitioin, but as it is dealing with a turntable, I thought I would read it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There lias been quite an agitation down there regarding the point where we make our crossing, not only at Pirate Harbour, which is further out to sea, but the same controversy has arisen both north and south of the present point of crossing. Both on the island and on the main line, we have had many pressing invitations to select our terminus at various points. After having studied the situation fully and had our officers examine it, we have been forced to the conclusion that there was nothing to 'be gained by making any change in the
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: crossing point, either on the island of Cape Bireton or on the mainland, and we have about decided to remain where we are. There are some advantages, perhaps, at Pirate Harbour, but on the whole we have been led to the conclusion that we had better stay where we are.
Have sea captains given their opinion about this matter?
I think we have been favoured with the opinions of almost everybody in that locality.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Several letters from sea captains that I have received point out one difficulty, that is, that a large steamer 280 feet long going across from Mulgrave to Point Tupper, with a current running four or five miles an hour, and sometimes ice running with it, forcing it broadside, would have great difficulty to make so sharp a point as Point Tupper for the terminus. Even the present comparatively small ferry boat has to be driven full steam in order to make that dock on the Point Tupper side of the Strait of Canso, thus subjecting both boat and wharf to damage, which they often sustain in this way. If there is a difficulty in docking a small steamer, there will necessarily be a much greater difficulty in docking this large steamer that it is proposed to put on that ferry. I would, therefore, suggest to the hon. minister that it might be prudent to experiment upon docking the new boat at Point Tupper before any great expenditure is made upon it as a permanent dock. I have five or six letters in my possession from sea captains who have navigated the Straits of Canso from boyhood to the present day. Men who have been in charge of almost all the steamers that ply around the Strait of Canso, and they are a unit in the opinion that it would be most difficult to dock a large boat at such a place as Point Tupper. I have already said that if the present small boat which plies on the ferry is not run at full speed to' avoid the ice and fight the current that is tending to bring her down stream she will fail to make her dock at that very narrow point and she will then be very likely to go on the ledge of rock on either side of the point. They, therefore, unanimously have answered several questions put to them by the town council of Hawkesbury as to whether the point called Grant's Point at the northern entrance of Hawkesbury harbour would uot toe a safer point at which to dock a large steamer. Their answers are unanimous that Grant's Point would be the safer of the two at which to dock a large steamer. Many railway men are also of the opinion that the government would lose no money upon all the works they have now established at Point Tupper. The round-house and all the paraphernalia for the Cape Breton terminus established there would not be lost money

In view of the fact that cars for repairs can he driven in there as a sort of yard just as they now are, while the dock would be in a safe, roomy place at the entrance of Hawkesbury harbour, one of the finest harbours in eastern Nova Scotia outside of Sydney and Halifax. As proof of its safety 1 may say that vessels frequenting the Straits of Canso in storms always make for that harbour. The government steamers always make for that harbour when they are on the coast of Cape Breton or of eastern Nova Scotia. When there is so much unanimity amongst men who are thoroughly versed in the navigation of the Strait of Canso. who are thoroughly posted on the currents and movements of the ice, where there is such unanimity as to the choice of Grant's Point as a point of landing for the ferry steamers, particularly as large a steamer as the proposed one, I think the hon. minister should hesitate a little and experiment upon the docking of that new boat on the Cape Breton side before a permanent dock is established. There is a vast sum of money about to be voted by parliament to establish a terminus on the Cape Breton side of the Strait of Canso. It happens that Port Hawkesbury is on the Inverness side of the line of demarcation between Richmond and Inverness, but that does not make any difference for me as to the point I suggest. If there is a safe point, even to the south of Point Tupper, it would not matter to me. If these sea captains had chosen such a point I would not have one word to say, but I consider it my duty, as representing a portion of the people of the Island of Cape Breton, which has a good deal to do with the road, to lay before the committee, and particularly before the Department of Railways and Canals, the opinions of all these sea-faring men, who are perfectly conversant with the navigation of the Strait of Canso.

I am quite prepared to admit that my hon. friend (Mr. McLennan) has no interest in presenting this view as he does, other than what he thinks would be in the public interest and for the advantage of the service. Therefore, what he has said, I am quite prepared to believe he is well convinced, is correct, but, at the same time ,T am bound to think there is not the entire unanimity among sea-faring men that my hon. friend apprehends.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, that when the value of the land was being fixed in the Exchequer Court by expropriation proceedings, there was a remarkable unanimity of opinion among a very large number of people around there that Point Tupper was the only possible place.

Mr. Chairman. I wish to say a few words on this question. We 131
have heard a good deal from my hon. and worthy friend from Inverness (Mr. McLennan). He has, however, only given the opinion of Port Hawkesbury. but it is well known that Port Hawkesbury has been for a number of years urging for railway accommodation. I think every person who knows the Strait of Canso will admit that the place at which to establish the dock, is not where it is narrow, but that it would be wise to go down where there is more room. The ice in the Strait of Canso must spread to make room for the steamer to pass through. The hon. gentleman says there is no place south of Tupper Point available.
I did not say that.

I think you did ; however, I am in the judgment of the committee. If I understood the hon. gentleman correctly he said there was a ledge of rock on each side of Tupper Point. However, we have not so many railway facilities in the county of Richmond that we can afford to lose what we have. It must be conceded by all that we have better harbours south of Point Tupper than can be found north of it. That is patent to all. It is true that there are lots of people from Port Hawkesbury who would try to get the steamer to go to that point, but, as I said before, to get clear of the ice, you must go to the south. I am well acquainted with the Strait of Canso. I have crossed the Strait of Canso many times since I was a little boy. I know every part of it. My life has been endangered several times and I have always known where to go to seek refuge, and to seek refuge I had to go south.
You had better keep clear of Point Tupper.

Point Tupper is bad enough.
To provide new superstructure for six spans Miramichi bridge, $72,000.
Would the hon. minister give us some explanation about this ?

The Miramichi, in company with all the other bridges along the line, has to be strengthened. We are happily situated here because we can turn these bridges to very good account and we propose to put them up on the Hillsboro' line in crossing at Charlottetown. We propose to make a division as between the Intercolonial Railway on the one hand and the Prince-Edward Island Railway on the other upon this basis. We estimate the cost of six new heavy spans of 200 feet each at $132,000. We value the old spans which we take out iat $60,000 and we put these old spans on the Hillsboro' bridge in Prince Edward Island.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
How old are these
spans ?

The spans are just as good as ever they were, only they are not considered strong enough for our purpose on the Intercolonial Railway, whereas they will be abundantly strong for the trains running on the Prince Edward Island road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will this bridge be wide enough to allow the Hillsboro' bridge to have a carriage drive on each side of the railway track ?
We propose to make it wide enough.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You will have to add to the old bridge to make it wide enough.
We will probably have to put on sides or something of that kind, but it is intended to make it amply wide for all purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you intend to have a carriage way on each side of the railway track in the Hillsboro' bridge ?

I have forgotten how the plans have been designed, but I think the track will run in the middle of the bridge and a carriage way on each side. It is nearly a year since I saw those plans, and I would not be absolutely certain as regards the arrangement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister is asking the Prince Edward Island government to pay about $10,000 a year for the building of this bridge. I presume that when he builds a bridge there he will build a good one.
Oh, we will build a good one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And not take an old, second-hand bridge from Miramichi over to Prince Edward Island and use it there ?
Oh, no.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And then patch it up. The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. There will be no patching up about it. We will give you as good a bridge as you would have if you got it wholly new out of the shop.
I hope you will, but it does not look much like it. That old bridge must be twenty years old.
Probably it is, and it will be good for a hundred years more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
And you charge the people of Prince Edward Island the full price of a new bridge.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. Oh, no.
You make them pay $10,000 a year out of their subsidy, and you ask them in addition to maintain the carriage way.
We are making a very nice arrangement for you.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think you are driving a very hard bargain so far as the people of Prince Edward Island are concerned.
Who has the contract for building the bridge, and was it let by public tender ?
Oh, yes, Mr. M. J. Haney.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not refer to the bridge in Prince Edward Island, but to the spans over the Miramichi.
We have not done anything with that yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why did not the minister adopt the same principle in reference to steel rails as he did in the case of this bridge, and only ask for the difference between the actual cost of the steel rails and the value of the rails he took up from the road ?
That is what I am doing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You have not done that in reference to the steel rails.
I beg your pardon, we have.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister has asked for $920,000 for steel rails for last year and this year, and if he only asked for the difference between the cost of the new rails and the value of the old, that would do for nearly two-thirds of the Intercolonial Railway.

What is the use of the hon. gentleman saying that. We discussed this matter of steel rails for three days, and the hon. gentleman now makes the same statement that he started out with the first or second day of the discussion. That has been all threshed out. I appeal to the hon. gentleman's sense of fair play not to revive the discussion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not reviving the discussion. The minister must know that he took a vote for the full price of the rails purchased.
I did not, Sir.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the minister tell me that he intends to buy over $600,000 worth of steel rails this year ?

I stated to the hon. gentleman that I proposed to buy 25,000 tons of rails, and from the market price of $32.60 I have deducted $15, and I have only asked now for $500,000, and I have to ask for $160,000 more, in order to make up that sum. If the hon. gentleman after three days debate does not understand any better, what is the use of talking.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the minister deducted that as he says, he is asking a good deal more than a million dollars for his rails this year.
Never mind, we will get all that again.
It would facilitate the passing of these items very much if we had the detailed plans and estimates before us.
I have given the estimate. We know what these things will cost.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not mean the final conclusion of the engineer, but the grounds of his estimate.
Will the minister let the Miramiehi bridge by tender ?
Undoubtedly. I am quite safe in saying that not a bridge has ever been constructed by this department that has not been done by tender, for either the superstructure or the other part.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We want some explanation of this item.

Included in this sum is an appropriation to cover the cost of twenty new locomotives which we are obtaining from the Canadian Locomotive Company of Kingston. The cost of these locomotives is $19,000 each, or $380,000 in all.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
What is the weight of those locomotives ?
The	MINISTER	OP	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Between eighty-two and ninety tons. They are being made upon the general specification which has been adopted by the department, and what are called consolidations-ten-wheeled.

You have the contracts	there, I suppose ?
The	MINISTER	OP	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I have, and all the papers.

You might leave them on the Table of the House. Just state the time the contract was made and the conditions. We do not want the details of the engines.
The	MINISTER	OP	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I think the time the contract 131i
was made has been already stated to the House. The correspondence will show that on the 16th of October, we passed the first order in council on the subject, authorizing the construction of fourteen locomotives. This was subsequently supplemented by an amending order making the number twenty.
What is the date of the amending order ?

The 28th of November. The minister recommended that the order in council of the 16th of October authorizing the purchase of fourteen locomotives from the Canadian Locomotive Works at Kingston be modified by increasing the number to twenty, and fixing the price at $19,000 each, delivered at Alontreal; the contract to be entered into with William Harty. The minister observed that under contracts recently entered into with American companies, the price was $14,425, and the customs duty added brought the total cost up to $19,555, or $555 more than the price proposed to be paid to the company.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman quite sure that the 16th of October is the date of the order in council ?
I am quite sure.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Well, I will draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that on the 18th of February, 1901, Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper drew the minister's attention to a certain document which had been circulated in the city of Kingston during the last election. At that time the acting Minister of Railways was in the city of Woodstock, and the Hon. Air. Harty in the city of Montreal. I find that these telegrams passed :
Montreal, November 5,	1900.-Hon. James
Sutherland, Woodstock, Ont.-Arrived here this morning, Windsor Hotel, will be here all day. Please answer my letter of Saturday by wire if possible. (Sgd.) William Harty.
Hon. Wm. Harty, Windsor Hotel, Montreal.- Have received no letter from you. (Sgd.) James Sutherland.
Hon. James Sutherland, Woodstock, Ont.-I mailed you a letter from Kingston Saturday night. You will likely receive It this afternoon. Wire answer to it if possible. (Sgd.) Wm. Harty.
Hon. William Harty, Windsor Hotel, Montreal. -Your offer to build twenty locomotive engines for the Intercolonial Railway accepted. Order in council already passed to this effect. (Sgd.) James Sutherland, acting Minister of Railways and Canals.
Montreal, November 5,	1900.-Hon. James
Sutherland, Woodstock, Ont.-Thanks for order. (Sgd.) William Harty.
These telegrams would indicate that nothing had been done previous to the 5th of November.
Oh, yes, the order in council for the fourteen locomotives had passed on the 16th of October.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then I find that on February 25th, 1901, the following question and answer were given in this House:

How many locomotives have been purchased by the Department of Railways and Canals or the government from January 1, 1897, up to the present time, for the Intercolonial Railway?
Of the total number of locomotives so purchased, how many have been purchesd in Canada and how many in the United States, and from what corporations or persons have such locomotives been purchased, and how many from each, and what is the amount or price paid or payable to each such corporation or person for such locomotives?

There have been no locomotives purchased by the department since the date mentioned, the 1st of January, 1897, though a number of locomotives and cars have been made as the result of tenders being asked for and of contracts entered into, and delivery has taken place. I am having a statement of them prepared which I can furnish if desired, but there have been none purchased in the ordinary sense.
I cannot quite make this out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: I presume the question was asked as distinguishing an ordinary transaction of purchase from the. obtaining of offers and the making of a contract for the manufacture and subsequent supply of locomotives at rates to be fixed. Mr. Sutherland's telegram, which was dated on the 5th of November, was evidently written under the impression that the order in council was for twenty locomotives. I said that on the 28th of November, the order in council had been passed, increasing the number to twenty. This is an error. The report from the minister went to council on that date, but the order in council did not actually pass until the 12th of December.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister has already stated that this correspondence is substantially correct; and what I cannot understand is, if it is substantially correct, how an order could be issued on the 16tli of October, when the offer was only made on the 3rd of November. On November 3rd, a letter was written to the acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) by Mr. Harty, stating that he expected to be in possession of the locomotive works in Kingston on the following Monday, and offering to build twenty locomotive engines for the Intercolonial Railway. This was written by a gentleman who did not then own the locomotive works and who apparently up to that tane had no control over them.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. We had the proposition long before that. They began to talk to us about their being able to get these works long before that. I find here a letter from Mr. Bucknell, dated as early as the 16th of August. He was acting for Mr. Harty, and at his request wrote stating that he is prepared to receive specifications for the locomotives, and on the 11th of August the specifications were sent to the Canadian Locomotive and Engine Company. The next document I have is the order in council of the 16th of October, authorizing fourteen locomotives to be contracted for with that company. I am quite sure that Mr. Harty must have made considerable progress with his purchase of the then Kingston Locomotive Works, or we would not have passed that order in council. We had his offer to build the locomotives and his assurance that he would have the works shortly within his control, and they did get into his control. All the transfers were probably completed before Mr. Harty wrote the telegram referred to.

Then, the language used in this letter of the 3rd of November is rather unfortunate. Mr. Harty says :
I expect to be in possession of the locomotive works in this city on Monday next, and now beg to offer you as follows:
That confirms my impression. Very likely the transfers were executed, and Mr. Harty was going to get possession in a day or two.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I fail to understand the point the hon. gentleman is trying to make. The Kingston Locomotive Works had been applying to the department for an order for some time. They had, I understand, got into difficulties and had not been able to make a contract with the department, although considerable correspondence had taken place. Afterwards the works went into liquidation, I think, and a receiver was appointed. An application was then made by Mr. Harty to the government to give the building of the locomotives to the Canadian institution in Kingston, of which he was about to obtain possession. The application was looked upon favourably, and I think the department intimated that it would be willing to give the preference to a Canadian institution which would tum out as good engines as could be had at other places and at the same figures. But there was considerable correspondence months before the date the hon. gentleman referred to, and we thought that if reputable men with some capital were able to conclude an arrangement with the estate for the purchase of the works, a contract could be made with them. The minister in charge of the department asked for power by order in council, or at any rate consulted the government, and was authorized, under the conditions I have mentioned, to give a preference to this institution, if it were able to turn

out the locomotives satisfactorily. Then some delay took place, as often happens in matters of this kind. I do not know that we had any occasion to know anything about the negotiations going on between the different parties. I am not sure who was associated with Mr. Harty or whether there were different parties trying to make arrangements to continue this work, but it was the wish of the government that the order should be given to a Canadiaii institution if possible. The communication was sent to me, as acting minister, addressed to Ottawa, when I was not here, and then I received the telegram. I remember that this agreement had been come to, and I am pretty sure the order in council was passed months before.
an option on the works. And while that option was in the hands of the other party, negotiations were being carried on by the government for the purchase of twenty locomotives. I do not know how the price was fixed, but I know that in all these things the price should be fixed by the ordinary rules of fair competition and tender openly called for. But, instead of that, a private arrangement is made with a party who owned no locomotive works and who could not even get an option on them at the time. And while this is the state of affairs a contract is made, as much as a contract could be made by an order in council, giving an order for twenty locomotives. After Mr. Harty gets the order, he completes the purchase.
It was passed on the 16th of October, but there was an understanding before that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The extraordinary position is this, that this man should have been in communication witb the government to furnish these locomotives before he had the least title to the property. The property belonged to the Bank of Montreal all the time he was negotiating with the government, and during that time another man had the option for the purchase of the property. On the 5th of November, the acting minister telegraphed his acceptance of Mr. Harty's offer to build twenty locomotives, and the next day-which was the day after the option to Mr. King had expired, he purchased the property. He was then in a position to go to the party from whom he was purchasing or to any bank in the country to get an advance of money for the purchase, having the contract from the government for twenty locomotives. And further, he does not need to furnish the capital for carrying on the work. One of the most extraordinary parts of the contract, if I understood the minister correctly, is that there are payments from time to time-progress estimates-on the work. Whoever heard of such a thing in the purchase of locomotives or cars before ? The contract was closed on the 5th of No. vember, two days before the election. On that day Mr. Harty gets word from the acting Minister of Railways, and the next day he makes a bargain, or one day after the option of Mr. King or the Bank of Montreal for the purchase of the property expired. This is the most extraordinary transaction, to use a very mild term, that I have heard of. The government negotiates with a party who, as I have stated, has not the slightest title to the property. It is true that Mr. Harty was formerly connected wi(th (the Kingston! Locomotive Works, being secretary or treasurer I believe. But the works had passed out of ' their hands into the hands of another party and that party had given to a third person
Supposing that to be the case- I do not know that it is-what is wrong With it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows that it Is the case, because the correspondence brought down by himself distinctly shows it.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CAAtaLS. I did not bring down any correspondence.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:

Why, he was making an arrangement with a party who had no title to the locomotive works.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, not to make an arrangement with one individual like Mr. Harty
What is the matter with Mr. Harty ?

I am not saying anything disparaging ,of Mr. Harty. He had a right to enter into an agreement with the government and make as good a bargain as he could. But fancy a government, two days before an election, bargaining with an individual to supply twenty locomotives and the minister solemnly getting an order in council passed authorizing him to enter into the contract.
