tlie government was bound so far as the arrangements could be made. We would like to see the whole correspondence. And I suppose the hon. minister intends to lay it on the Table before he asks us to pass this item. I have not heard whether a contract was actually made and signed for the construction of these engines, but if it was, we would like to see it.
I think the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) assumes altogether too much when he says that he knows all about the negotiations between the parties for the control of the Kingston Locomotive Works.
I never said anything about that.
The hon. gentleman is pretending to say that Mr. Harty had no connection with this matter up to this day.
Yes, he says so himself.

From a legal standpoint perhaps he had not. But the hon. gentleman must remember that we are not acquainted with the position of affairs between the different parties to the estate, nor do I think that makes any material difference ; because during the last session of parliament when this matter was under discussion, I understood the minister to say that he had given orders to the Kingston Locomotive Works which they were unable to fill, and for that reason he was compelled to buy from manufacturers in the United States, but he would be very glad to purchase locomotives from the Kingston works if they were able to fill the orders. That statement was made publicly to the whole country and the world. The statement that negotiations were going on was public property, the knowledge that the government were prepared to give these works a preference was known to every person as well as to Mr. Harty. There was nothing secret about it, there was no special information given to Mr. Harty. I am not sure that Mr. Harty was the first man to conduct the negotiations. My recollection is that Mr. Harty had not been connected with the works for several years previous to that time. I understand that the citizens and workingmen of Kingston who were out of employment at that time, had appealed to Mr. Harty, who had been somewhat successful in the previous management, to help them to re-establish these works. But my hon. friend would give the impression to the House that Mr. Harty was in possession of some special knowledge that enabled him to have advantage in purchasing these works. I do not think that it was considered any great snap. They had been interviewing manufacturers and people that had capital throughout this country, and per-

haps across the line, trying to get them interested in these works, as I understand ; and the government policy was declared openly and above-board that whenever they were in a position to go on with the works and furnish locomotives the government were prepared to give an order. That declaration was made a year ago. I remember well that months before that, I think during the last session, Mr. Harty was here and told me that on account of ill-health he did not feel himself equal to taking hold of the management of the works, and that he was endeavouring to interest other capitalists in this matter. X have not the slightest doubt that that was correct, and that these negotiations were going on. Some delay took place. I had no idea the Bank of Montreal was interested, nor do X think it makes any difference. In my opinion the government did their duty in the matter, and I am not ashamed at all, but proud to know that the government adopted that policy of giving encouragement towards reopening these works by promising orders on equal terms. I think the government were careful to protect the country's interests when they accepted the offer to make locomotives as good as can be made in any other part of the world, and at as low a price.

I have heretofore given the government credit for being rather shrewd in elections, but I am forced to admit, after hearing the argument of the hon. gentleman, that they have been a little slack in this contract at Kingston. We know about a year ago there was a good deal of discussion, and the Minister of Railways and Canals was condemned for giving contracts to some of the American manufacturers. It appears strange now, if this order was passed on the 16th of October, giving this order to the Kingston works, that the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton), who was a candidate and in the midst of an election, and the Hon. Mr. Harty, who is a pretty good politician, would not have got an inkling of this order in council giving them the contract to manufacture these engines in Kingston. It seems strange, knowing the great advantage the hon. gentleman took of it after the 5th of November, because I find this was circulated in Kingston :
Locomotive works bought-Hon. Wm. Harty Kingston's friend-Has orders for 32 locomotives -20 for the government and 12 for Mackenzie & Mann-Where was the Conservative help for the city on this occasion-Read the government's contracts below, and thank Liberals for redeeming a big industry.
You see the energy they put forth in order that the workingmen of Kingston might know that the works were to be resumed by this order of the government. The order in council of the 16th of October, notwithstanding the statement of the Minister of
Railways and Canals, does look to me as being a little bit fishy. If the documents are brought down and they prove that statement, I will take back what I say.
I can give the hon. gentleman the documents now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I find that the statement made by the minister to-night that the amending order in council was passed on the 28th of November
I corrected that by saying that was the date reported from the acting minister. The order itself did not get to council until December 12th.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then the statement made by the minister on the 18th of February was this :
An order in council was thereupon passed on October 16th authorizing a contract to be entered into, and later on, December 22nd, the last contract was executed between the government and the Kingston company.
For what ? For fourteen locomotives ?
No, for twenty.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the statement as made by Mr. Harty in Kingston that there was an arrangement entered into was not a correct statement ?
He saw the telegram from the acting minister, who had the impression, I suppose, that the order was for twenty. He was in Woodstock, he was not here to refer to it, but he knew the order had passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Now, if the Kingston Locomotive Works manufacture as good locomotives as were manufactured in Kingston previous to the collapse, I am sure the hon. gentleman will have no cause for complaint. I know from my own knowledge that the Kingston Locomotive Works manufactured good engines. They had been used on the Michigan Central Railroad. I watched them carefully for years, and I have inquired into the way these engines worked, and I know they gave satisfaction to the Michigan Central Company. I have been assured on every occasion that these engines are as good as the company have had in use. Now, with respect to the price. According to the contract with Mr. Harty, he says he will guarantee to manufacture these engines for $500 less than any manufacturer in the United States or Canada can supply them.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. With the duty added.
Has the bon. gentleman inquired what the same class of engine can he procured for from other manufacturers ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And does he assure us that he can get engines at Kingston for $500 less than anywhere else ?

I can assure the hon. gentleman that the price is $19,000, which the government engaged to pay to the Kingston company, and is $555 less than the price that we were paying for precisely the same class of locomotives, with the duty added.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That must be some years ago.	.

That is not some years ago. $14,485 is the price of locomotives of the same description that we were getting made for us in the United States. At that time they were not then delivered. AVe added to that a duty of 35 per cent, which would amount to $5,070. This added to the American price would bring the engine up to $19,555 ; and we made a contract for $19,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I say that must have been some time ago, because the hon. gentleman has stated that they have purchased no engines since the 1st of January, 1897.

We had engines which were being made then under contract. I explained that, I said I would furnish the return it desired, and would bring down a list of those that had been made for us under contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think we ought to have the statements as promised on the 25th of February, so that we may be in a position to judge.
I can get it for the hon. gentleman ; also the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In favour of the Canadian Locomotive and Engine Works.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: While on the 5th we have the telegraph of the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals accepting a tender to build twenty locomotives.
AVliat difference does that make ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that in the matter of the locomotive works at Kingston, it is impossible to please hon. gentlemen, because, turn whichever way we will and do whatever we may, an attempt is made to make political capital against the member for Kingston and the Liberal party in reference to them.
If my hon. friend will allow me, I would say to him that I have no objection whatever to the works being gone on with at Kingston.
You did have.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken. He should not put words in my mouth that I never uttered. I want to understand the transfer. I would be very glad to see the work done at Kingston.

I will see if I cannot make the hon. gentleman understand it. When I was first elected, nearly the first work that I had to do was to attempt to see if a contract could not be got from this government for the building of locomotives at Kingston. I do not remember the exact time, and although I cannot give exact dates, l am going to give truly in substance what has taken place in reference to this matter, and I will challenge successful contradiction of anything that I shall say. But I shall not be able, because I am speaking entirely from memory, having no notes, to give the exact dates at which the occurrences to which I have referred took place. After the election of 1896, I think some time in 1897, I attended upon the government and tried to get a contract for some locomotives to be built at Kingston. I succeeded. The contract was not a large one. Unfortunately, the works at Kingston were in, to some extent, a state of decay.
They had not the capital to do it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
They were not able to do, in the course of their undertakings, what they were expected to do, and so a little dissatisfaction resulted because the locomotives were not finished in the time specified
in their contract. Hon. gentlemen opposite and not only the Conservatives in Kingston, but all over the country, were charging the government with refusing to give work to the Kingston Locomotive Works, and capital was attempted to he made against us because of this alleged refusal on the part of the government to do that. I asserted that the government were willing to prefer Canadian manufacturers, other things being equal and the price being reasonable. I stated that, in this House in 1897 or 189S, and I recollect distinctly the then hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Charles Tupper) saying that the government were perfectly right, in giving Canadian factories work, giving them a price and adding to the price the duty that an individual would have to pay if he brought locomotives over from the other side. That statement seemed to meet with the approval of hon. members opposite, and with the approval of the whole House. Things went from bad to worse with the Canadian Locomotive Works, or with the Canadian Locomotive and Engine Company, as the corporation was known. Let me state what Mr. Harty's connection with the matter was. Years before Mr. Harty was the managing director of that company and he managed it so successfully that he made money out of it for the shai*e-holders and for himself. He managed it so successfully that he and the other stockholders, among whom was the late Sir George Kirkpatrick, were able to sell their stock to Scotch capitalists at 150. The stock then went into the hands of people outside of Kingston, the works were being managed by these people, and from time to time at a loss. In February, 1900, the company was put into liquidation under the Joint Stock Companies Winding Up Act. The acting liquidator was Mr. Riddell, of Montreal, and another gentleman was associated with him. The Bank of Montreal had nothing to do with the company other than that they were creditors, and as such the inspector of the Bank of Montreal was made one of the inspectors in connection with the winding up. There were three inspectors and two liquidators acting in connection with the liquidation. Early in the history of the liquidation Mr. Harty made an offer for that concern and it had no more to do with politics than the ordinary purchase of an article in a store. Mr. Harty knew what could be done with that business. He knew the value of the plant and of the property there ; he knew the cost in round figures to be $300,000, and believing that it would not realize anything near its value lie offered $50,000 for the plant and property, and $10,000 for the material on hand, making a total of $60,000. The liquidators would not look at it, and his standing offer of $60,000 remained during the entire summer. It ran along until about two months before the 7th of November-the date of the elections has been dragged into this-when

the liquidators gave an option to some one at a figure above $50,000. I do not remember the name, but the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says it was Mr. King.

I got the name from the correspondence brought down by the acting minister.
Hon. Mr. S UTHERLANI). There is no secret about it.

The option was given to some one at a price exceeding $60,000, and it was thought this gentleman was not going to exercise his option. Now, when this was a going concern 300 men were employed and it meant everything to the merchants of Kingston, and to the working people of Kingston, and no matter which party was in power, the people were anxious to have that option determined one way or the other, and some one went to New York to try to induce this person to give up his option before the expiration of the time. I do not know whether Mr. King was in New York or not, but at all events the person who had control of it was in New York at the time. He would not give up his option which had been given him long before and the date of which did not expire until Monday, the 5th November. Consequently no one could get the concern. But it was understood for weeks before that if that gentleman did not exercise his option, Mr. Harty's offer of $50,000 would be accepted. We all believed that Mr. Harty would get the concern. The elections were announced after these negotiations had begun, and all this talk about getting the control into the hands of Mr. Harty, and the Kingston-ians, took place before the elections were announced. As soon as the elections were announced the cry was raised against me that the Liberal party were instrumental in closing these works, that all the disaster that would come to Kingston by reason of these 300 men being out of employment was due to the Liberal government because they would not give contracts to Canadians. The liquidators carried the concern on under the direction of the court to the extent of manufacturing the materials on hand, but they would not enter into new contracts. At this time and before the elections the works were actually closed, and it was made a cry against me, as I have said, that the Liberal party had been instrumental in closing the works..
Would the hon. gentleman say who Mr. E. J. B. Pense is ?

Yes. He is the proprietor of the British Whig in Kingston. He is a prominent man in Kingston and takes an interest as owner of that journal in every enterprise that is calculated to promote the welfare and prosperity of the city.
Politics included.

Yes, polities included. He is the editor of the Liberal paper, the British Whig, a paper that does credit to the city it is published in, and which is quoted very largely by newspapers all over the country, 'and, sometimes an independent streak seizes Mr. Pense and that is applauded by hon. gentlemen opposite so that they endorse his opinions to some extent at least. As I have stated, the cry was raised that the Liberal government were instrumental in closing these works and if publicity was given to the fact that Mr. Harty succeeded in buying the works, and had secured a contract for building these locomotives it was simply to meet the arguments that had been used by the other side for weeks before. That is a plain history of the transaction. As a matter of fact I do not think the announcement at so late a date did the Liberal candidate a particle of good. A counter proclamation, if you can, call it such, was 'issued, saying that Mr. Harty had not bought the concern, that the whole thing was a fake, but finally it was found that what we said all along was true, and that we had the interests of Kingston at heart. Mr. Harty for his own purpose and as a matter. of investment in a business which he knew a good deal about, got this property cheap and every one in Kingston was glad and applauded him for his enterprise. Where is the blame in that. I cannot see it. Mr. Birkett is a gentleman- the minister read the wrong name, because it was a misprint-who had been in the employ of the concern with Mr. Harty, in the old days, and he afterwards continued in the employ of the liquidators. The government were just as willing to give contracts to one party as to the others, so long as it was a Canadian industry and so long as they had the capital and ability to carry out these contracts.
What capital had Mr. Harty ?
Why, Mr. Harty is a wealthy man. Does any one say that he is not a wealthy man ?
On the basis of the financial structure built up by this contract.

No. Mr. Harty was
wealthy before, and there are hon. gentlemen in this House who know it. Mr. Harty was ready to buy out the concern entirely on his own responsibility. He did not want any of us who were willing to go in with him. He was quite convinced that money could be made out of it, but after he purchased, he formed a connection with Mr. Haney, whose name I hear in connection with large contracts, and who, I understand, is a wealthy man. Mr. Harty and Mr. Haney are running the concern, and although they have formed a joint stock company, I believe, in Toronto, so far as I know.

the stock has not been offered to any one. It is a pure business transaction. If the transaction had not taken place as it did, no doubt political capital would have been made out of it, because the allegation that the government had closed down the industry because they would not give work to a Canadian establishment, would have succeeded to a very great extent.
I state as absolutely true that there has been from the very first, ever since I have been a member of this House, an honest desire to have that Canadian industry reestablished at Kingston, and to get work for it; and every attempt that has been made and the success that has attended it, has been misrepresented by some hon. gentlemen opposite and by their press throughout the country. A most unfair attempt has been made from the beginning to make political capital out of the matter. Conservatives and Liberals alike have been desirous to obtain orders for that establishment as soon as it was able to carry them out. At the present time, at the heel of the hunt, When Mr. Harty has the work in successful operation-and if he does not do it successfully, he must answer for the consequences-and when all is going on smoothly, to attempt to open up the matter in order to make political capital out of it, is most unfair.

Most of what the hon. gentleman has said is no doubt quite true. These Kingston works were hawked about almost everywhere, and offered for $50,000. They were offered to me amongst others for that amount. Some people brought them to my notice and asked me to join. I figured over the matter. I am not anxious to take hold of any works which depend for their success on government contracts; 1 have always avoided that. To carry on these works and build sixteen or twenty locomotives entailed an expenditure of practically $380,000 in addition to the $50,000 of capital, which was a small thing to raise. At that particular time money was perhaps a little scarce, and it was hard to make a contract with a bank for sucih a large amount of money for one transaction. The one thing I blame the government for in connection with this matter is this. If they had informed other contractors before that date that they were willing to make a departure and advance 80 per cent on progress estimates, these works would never have failed, as the hon. member for Kingston says they failed, for want of capital. To take a contract to build twenty engines meant that the company liad to get a bank credit of $250,000 or $300,000. Assuming that the company made 10 per cent profit, which would be a reasonably small profit, they would deduct $38,000 from the $380,000, the total amount of the contract. So that they would only require to have a capital of $38,000 to
finance this contract. Iv.mout having the details of the contract, and being able to submit these to an expert, I do not propose to say anything as to the price of the engines. I will assume that that is all right; but as to advancing 80 per cent on progress certificates, that is an entirely new departure. I am not saying that it is a bad thing. For myself I am delighted to see the works re-established in Kingston. But that contract was made on the 5th of November, two days before the election, and it assured the success of the government candidate in Kingston. Without that contract having been made at that time, I do not think the hon. member for Kingston would now be in this House.
I do not agree with that.
That is my opinion.

Your opinion was that I was beaten already.
Mr, OSLER. It was because this contract had not come out then. Personally, however, I am glad that the works have been established, and I hope they will be successful.

There is one point which I want to make perfectly clear. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier lays great stress on the point that the order in council which passed when my hon. friend was negotiating for the work was only for fourteen engines, and that I said in the telegram to Mr. Harty that the order in council was for twenty engines. I was under the impression that the number was the number mentioned in his letter. There was nothing secret about it, and no intention to do anything wrong. What I did say in the presence of the premier was that the policy of the government was to give an order for twenty engines. Evei-y-thing was done in a business way and aboveboard and there is nothing to he ashamed of. If getting the consent of the government to increase the number by six had the result of re-establishing the Kingston Locomotive Wrorks, I am only proud of what took place, and do not think that the people of Kingston or any of those employed in those works will agree with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. I do not dispute the telegram, because I knew that the government had consented to increase the number to twenty if the company would place themselves in a position to successfully open the works and fulfil the contract; and if the government could get a locomotive built in Canada at a less price or on as favourable terms as anywhere else, I want to know why they should not do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Why did you not do it years before ?
41^3

As to the subsequent terms which the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) tries to find fault with, they simply amount to this. Long after the election, I suppose, there were negotiations with the department for the contract and certain propositions were accepted. There is no occasion to find fault with the contract as now made. Everything was done openly and above-board, and when the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) had admitted that people went to him, knowing him to be a wealthy man with plenty of capital at his disposal for investment, and asked him to join with them in taking over these works, and that he knew perfectly well the policy of the government with regard to this matter, that altogether disposes of his argument. Had any proposition been made by the hon. geu-tleman, no doubt he would have received the same consideration as that which came afterwards from those who took possession of the works. The point I wish to make perfectly clear is that there was no secret understanding between Mr. Harty and myself for political or other purposes. If these men succeeded in concluding their negotiations before the election and the Liberal party got the benefit, it was only a small measure of justice done them for the improper criticisms of my hon. friend and the government during the previous year or two, and I am glad he igot the benefit.

The hon. gentleman says that everybody knew the principle on which the government was acting. Did the hon. gentleman who had the option on this property know that the government would pay progress estimates ?
Did he ask for any such contract ?
If he had known that there was any possibility of his obtaining such a contract, he would have closed his option long before he gave it up, and have gone on with the business.
The party who bought had no knowledge that he could make such a contract. Was it not subsequent to his entering into negotiations that he made this arrangement ?

I contend that everybody did not know the policy of the government. The man who held the option did not know it or he would have entered into the contract just as well as Mr. Harty did. The hon. member for South Oxford says there is nothing to toe ashamed of, but there never was a political job yet which he was ashamed of, and I do not wonder that he was not ashamed of this, nor will the country wonder either. What is strange about the whole matter is the way these government contractors bob up now and again just in the Mr. TAYLOR.
right time to get control of this thing or the other, and then shortly afterwards get some government contract. Mr. Haney comes in.
He was not there until long after the election in connection with this matter.
I understood the hon. member for Kingston to say, in answer to my question as to how Mr. Harty could finance this scheme, that Mr. Harty had Mr. Haney at his back.
Yes, but Mr. Haney came in later. He was not there nor was his name known in any shape or form before the election.
How does the hon. gentleman know that Mr. Haney had no correspondence with Mr. Harty about it ?
I dare say he knew Mr. Harty's transactions and how he intended financing, but Mr. Haney was not connected with the thing then.
It seems passing strange that Mr. Haney should come in at the opportune time to helpi Mr. Harty to finance the scheme.
The contract was made with Haney, Harty and Birmingham.

Yes, and made at this opportune time, and it seems to have turned out very remunerative to the parties interested. And Mr. Haney comes at the opportune time with Mr. Charleson, of telegraph fame. He seems to have received slices of government money from various sources. The hon. gentleman says that this contract was under way for nearly a year. But the same thing was stated in connection with the Glergue contract, and what ;s peculiar about these contracts is that they come to a head just at the time the elections are on. They may have been under way for six months or a year or two previous, but, they do not reach a final conclusion until the elections are on, when it is of the greatest importance that these people should enter into contracts with the government which will be of use to them in assisting their political friends. Does any one pretend that this contract did not help the hon. member for Kingston ?
I say it did not.

Will the hon. gentleman pretend that in a dead place like Kingston, if he goes on a platform before the election, and says we have succeeded, through the influence of the government, in establishing a work that will give employment to 300 men
The reason it did not influence the election in Kingston is because the hon. gentleman's friends said it was all a fake.

But tlie hon. gentleman had a telegram saying that a contract was entered into for twenty locomotives and that in addition they had a contract for twelve more, which would mean an expenditure of about $1,200,000.
Your newspapers contended that there was not a word of truth in these statements.

The people believed the hon. gentleman rather than the newspapers. Will any one pretend that to tell the people of Kingston, where there was not employment enough for labour, that a very important work was to be started, which would give employment to 200 or 400 or 500 men, would not help them ? We had an example in Owen Sound when the hon. member for North Grey was running his election. We know that the announcement of the government contract there resulted in buying up that constituency.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the constituency of North Grey can be bought V

I could tell the hon. gentleman a little more about it that he thinks the outside world knows. I happen to have some affidavits in my possession which will bear out what I say, and the less the hon. gentleman says about that election the better for himself and his reputation. I have no doubt that this contract did in Kingston what the other promised contract did in North Grey. It resulted in carrying the election, and that election was carried as corruptly as if you went out with the money in your hand and bought up the election man by man. We saw the same course pursued with regard to the Olergue steel rail contract. That contract was under way nearly a year, but strange to say it only reached its culmination at that particular time, when the writs were issued for the election, and was only then given out to the world. These things do appear to disinterested people as not being business transactions carried out on the ordinary lines and on ordinary business principles. Was there a deposit asked ? Not a dollar. So that if the parties had seen fit to back out, there was nothing to hold them to their contract. Was there a deposit asked in the case of the Clergue contract ? Not a dollar, and it reached its culmination just as the elections were on.
You say that we concealed it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I say it was concealed, because the outside world did not know anything about it.

The hon. gentleman can hardly reconcile those two propositions-that we kept the thing a secret, and on the other
hand, that we used it to carry the constituency. _
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was kept secret between the government and the party with whom they negotiated until the opportune time. Not one of the newspapers in Canada knew nothing about the negotiations until the writs were- issued.
Yes, months before.
What paper ?
The Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) made a speech at the Soo long before the election. It was made public in every paper, and it was discussed in newspapers and on the platform everywhere.
The hon. gentleman cannot find a newspaper in the city of Toronto that contained that announcement.
It is easy for a man to make a statement-
At first, this speech was made back in Muskoka, but now it is at the Soo. It is strange that we, who live in that country, heard nothing about it.
I have made the statement before, and I make it now. There were hundreds of thousands who read it, and thousands who heard the speech. There was nothing secret about it.

I have not seen anybody except the hon. gentleman himself who knew of it, though most other persons are readers of the press as well as he. This is too important a question to be kept out of the press if it had been announced at any place where the press could learn of it. Nothing was known of it until the elections came on.
And yet the hon. gentleman says that we kept it secret till the present time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have evidently failed to make myself understood. I said that it was kept secret until the opportune time for the government. One arrangement was made on the 5th of November, while the election was on the 7th ; while the other was made on the 9th October, the day the writs were issued. And when we look into it and see that it was all done in this unbusiness-like way, it makes the transaction look all the worse. I think the country will express its displeasure
We have no occasion to be very much afraid of the country on these questions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Had these things been known, badly as the government were de-

feated in Ontario, they would have fared far worse. And no doubt more will be heard of this matter when the proper time comes.
That is what the hon. gentleman said before, but his promise was not realized.
But the hon. gentleman was defeated in Ontario.
But Ontario Is not the whole Dominion. It is a great province, but it is not always represented by great men.
I think its representatives will compare favourably with those of the hon. gentleman's province.
With me, no doubt, but not with those who sit behind us.

I wish to reply to the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) who has charged us with trying to make political capital out of the Kingston Locomotive Works. I am afraid the hon. gentleman has forgotten the records of this House. If he will look at the debate which took place on February, 1898, he will see that it was not hon. gentlemen on this side, but his own colleague who tried to make* capital out of these works. On the 1st March, 1898, there was a provincial election. The local member for Kingston made a statement while speaking in that city which was reported in the Kingston Whig, the hon. gentleman's own paper, as follows
I think the workingmen have some knowledge of the interest I have taken in them for a number of years. I have never lost sight of the desirability of aiding the workingmen. Mayor Livingstone suggested to me the manufacturing of locomotives for the Intercolonial Railway, and that we do something to get the contract for Kingston. I wrote Mr. Blair (Minister of Railways and Canals) and have just received a telegram to-day. He says he intends giving Kingston works the opportunity to build locomotives for that railway, the specifications for which will be sent at once. My desire is to give home manufacturers the first preference, and I am glad the work is coming here.
That is right.

Wait a moment, the Globe of the 1st February, reporting Mr. Harty's speech, said :
Before sitting down, he read a telegram from the Hon. Mr. Blair announcing that the Kingston Locomotive Works had received an order to construct three locomotives for the Intercolonial Railway, an announcement that was greeted with great applause.
Now, we will see what the hon. minister had to say about that. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) asked a question in this House, and this is the question and the answer :
To what parties have letters or telegrams been sent announcing that such contract had been given to the Kingston Locomotive Works?
The reply of the Minister of Railways was :
No such letter or telegram has been sent as is referred to in this sub-question.
That means that the statement made by the Globe that Mr. Harty read a telegram sent from the minister was not correct, because the minister tells us that no such telegram was sent. So, instead of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Britton) charging the Conservatives with endeavouring to make political capital out of these works, the records show that the friends of the hon. gentleman are those who have endeavoured to make political capital In this way.

I have had but a short time to look over the correspondence. Will the hon. member answer a few questions. First, dealing with what the hon. gentleman said about the public knowledge of the order in council of the 16th October, I notice that there is no public announcement until the very day after Mr. King's option expired. That expired on Monday the 5th November, and the announcement was made the day afterwards. I see no correspondence in which Messrs. Haney, Harty and Bermingham proposed that there should be an advance payment of 80 per cent as the work is progressing. In fact I find the order in council of November 28th in which the contract
That was the date of the report. If the hon. gentleman will turn over the page, he will see that the order was passed on the 12th December.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is a memorandum which recommends the giving of an order for fourteen locomotives, which may be modified by increasing the number to twenty, to the Canadian Locomotive and Engine Company, for $19,000 each, delivered on the Intercolonial at Montreal, the said locomotives to be single expansion consolidated freight engines, a contract to be entered into by Mr. Wm. Harty, who has acquired the property of the company. And it gives the type of the engine, but nothing about the progress estimates.
That was later.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then there was a memorandum of the 28th November, 1900, approved by His Excellency on the 12th December :
On a memorandum dated 28th November, 1900, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, recommending that the order in council dated 16th October, 1900, which authorized the purchase of fourteen locomotives for the Intercolonial Railway from the Canadian Locomotive and Engine Company of Kingston be modified by increasing the number to twenty and fixing the price at

$19,000 each, to be paid on progress certificates up to 80 per cent of the value of material supplied and work done on conditions to be prescribed by the minister.
Then the department authorized the contract to be entered into with Mr. Win. Harty, Michael Haney and Cornelius Ber-mingham. There seems to be no correspondence at all with reference to the change, the recommendation by the minister that the contract be given to these parties instead of to Mr. Harty.

I apprehend that would all be arranged orally. The hon. gentleman will see that the report to council of the 28tb of November was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was acting for ;me in my absence, and it was likely the subject of oral discussion, because we have no written records in the department relating to the subject. The hon. member has been furnished with all we have. It would be the subject of personal interview, and of an amendment to the order at the time of its passage on the 12th of December.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is very inadvisable that contracts of this importance should be conducted by the department orally alone. The proper way is to have the negotiations made in writing. Further, I see there is a letter from Mr. Pottinger to the deputy minister, dated the 6th of February, 1901 :
I have your letter dated January 29th inclosing a copy of the agreement with Messrs. Wm. Harty and others for twenty freight locomotives to be built at Kingston. The specification has a new clause in it, No. 12, by which 20 per cent of the price of the locomotives is to be paid in monthly instalments.
I suppose he means 80 per cent.
We formerly paid on delivery of each machine, retaining a certain portion of the price to cover failures of the engine afterwards for a time. As we are to tpay for the locomotives before delivery, will it not be advisable to require the contractors to effect an insurance on the material at their expense, so as to protect the railway from loss? The 8th clause provides for the replacing of anything damaged or destroyed, but it is perhaps a question whether that is sufficient protection or not.
Then, here is the minister's answer, through L. K. Jones, secretary :
I have to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of the 6th instant, relative to the contract recently entered into with Messrs. Wm. Harty et al., for the supply and delivery of twenty locomotives for the Intercolonial Railway, by which you suggest that, as the railway is to pay for the locomotives before delivery, it would be advisable to require the contractors to effect, at their own expense, an insurance on the material in order to protect the railway from loss. In reply, I am, by direction, to inform you that it is too late now to act on your suggestion, and that the clause No. 12, to which you refer, was inserted in the specification in this regard by the minister himself, with a full knowledge of the facts of the case,
he, no doubt, considering the 8th clause, also referred to in your said letter, quite sufficient.
Any protest from Mr. Pottinger receives the proper snub that it ought from the minister. I see also that the contract is not for twenty locomotives, it is for twenty-two.
We contracted for two afterwards, they are separate contracts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see that the contract has been transferred, or allowed to be transferred, from Harty, Haney and Ber-mingham, to the Canadian Locomotive Works, by order in council. What I particularly object to is that there is no correspondence with reference to the change, and no written proposals from the parties entering into an important contract like this, and no report from the officers of his department as to the value which was placed upon them. There is nothing hut a statement that he has purchased locomotives for a certain price, and after deducting duty, they come to a price within $400 or $500 of the price that is being paid by him elsewhere. I also object to the secrecy in which the whole of this transaction was involved. The whole transaction appears to me to be of a suspicious character.
Carried.
No, there is over a million dollars for cars.

I do not want to force the hon. gentleman to remain any longer to-night. I suppose the summer will be long enough to enable us to get through the Items. I move that the committee rise and report progress. We cannot report any resolutions, for we have not passed any.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman lay on the Table to-night, or early In the morning, the correspondence in reference to the cars. I moved for the papers long ago, and they ought to have been on the Table long ago.
I don't think the hon. gentleman moved for anything.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will read the order if the hon. gentleman doubts it.

I have been anxious to furnish all that information. If the hon. gentleman will find the order I will be pleased to stand corrected. But I have not been aware to the present moment that the hon. gentleman had moved for any such papers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will read it.

How many locomotives have been purchased for the Department of Railways and Canals ? How many passenger cars? How many freight

ears? The total number of locomotives so purchased? How many have been purchased in Canada and how many in the United States? From what corporation or persons have such locomotives been purchased, and how many from each, and what is the amount of price paid or payable to each corporation or person for such locomotives? Also the total number of passenger cars and freight cars.
That is a question. The hon. gentleman was told that if he wished for a return and moved for it, I would bring it down. But the hon. gentleman never moved for it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman promised to lay that information on the Table.
No, I said if it was desired I would bring down a return, but I did not undertake to give that information, all of it, in answer to a question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I put a question as to the number of locomotives purchased by the department since the date mentioned, the 1st of January, 1897, the number of locomotives and cars that had been made as a result of the tenders being asked for and the contracts entered into, and the hon. gentleman says he has a statement prepared which he can furnish.
The hon. gentleman never moved for a return for any of these.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I asked for them, and I should judge from the answer I got that there were none purchased.

No, but a number were being made, and if the hon. gentleman desired a list of all these I would furnish it. But I would not undertake to furnish to those questions an answer which would necessarily be so voluminous.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman can end the controversy if he will undertake to lay anything he may have on the Table so that we can consider it three or four hours in advance. Will the hon. minister do that 1

I do not want the hon. gentleman to put me in the wrong when I was not in the wrong. I will be very glad to furnish the hon. gentleman with the information, and if he asks me now to bring it down I shall have it prepared and brought down at the earliest possible moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There is an item lower down of $450,000 in connection with the Murray harbour branch and Hillsboro' bridge. If there are any documents which the hon.
Mr. HAGGART
minister thinks we would be liable to ask for in connection with this matter, possibly he might give the subject a few moment's reflection and have these documents brought down, because we will get along a great deal faster if we have these documents.
If the hon. gentleman will intimate that he wants me to bring down any papers in connection with these estimates I will do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is the large item of $450,000 in connection with the Murray harbour branch an regard to which there may be some documents. If be had them before we attack the item, it will enable us to shorten our questions very much.

Yes, I will bring down whatever we have.
Some resolutions reported.

The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
